speechtext: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 232) to further amend the Manitoba Grain Act, 1900. He said : This Bill proposes to ameud what is kuown as the Manitoba Grain Act, which is an Act of very great importance in regard to the transaction of the grain business and the shipment of grain in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. It has been the subject of a good deal of consideration in this House and it has been found an extremely complicated subject and one in regard to which it was very difficult to reconcile the conflicting interests and conflicting views of different parts of the community. However, further discussion and experience have rendered it possible to bring the parties who are interested, the shippers, the buyers and the railway companies, rather more into harmony in their views. During the present session the Grain-growers Association of the west sent delegates to the city of Ottawa and they discussed the subject here during my absence with representatives of the grain dealers and the railway companies, and the result has been that they have practically arrived at an arrangement as to what would be fairly satisfactory mutually in the way of an amendment to the existing law. I may say that there is little doubt that the law as it stands at the present time is capable of improvement. I think the Bill which I am about to present and which represents something of a compromise arrangement entered into by the parties concerned will be a very great improvement in the direction of bringing about harmony and general contentment. The specific details of the Bill will, of course, be discussed further on the second reading and in committee, but in the meantime I will give a brief statement of what the Bill purposes to do. Sections 1 and 2 deal with the interpretation of the terms used in the Bill. Section 3 provides for the appointment of deputy commissioners. There is now a grain commissioner who has very considerable duties to perform under the Act and it has been found quite impossible for one man to do all tne work. Of course the work, owing to he rapid increase in the production anu shipment of grain from Manitoba and the North-west Territories, has enormously increased. It is generally admitted that more than one officer is required. Section 4 makes provision that what are known as track buyers of grain shall take out licenses. Section 5 makes provisions regarding the duties of

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
weighmasters. It requires the weignmasters to keep a record of the fact when a car is leaking or in bad order. Section 6 deals with the time of rendering statements by warehousemen owning terminal public elevators. Section 7 gives the commissioner power to deal with disputes regarding applicants for elevator sites. Section 8 removes the provision which gives the commissioner discretion respecting the keeping of an account of the grain received, stored and shipped. Section 9 provides that the Act shall not require the receipt of grain where there is not sufficient accommodation in the elevator. Section 10 repeals the provision which in the present Act makes the holder of a receipt not liable for storage charges after the expiration of seven days from the giving of the notice requiring his grain to be shipped. Section 11 deals with the power of any person having grain stored in the elevator to order a car to be placed at such elevator. Section 12 amends the provisions relating to the duty of the warehousemen when grain is out of condition. Section 13 deals with the duty of the warehousemen in furnishing statements to the commissioner. Section 14 provides for the erection of flat warehouses. Section 15 defines the time within which any person who has procured a site is required to commence the erection of his elevator or warehouse.. Section 16 makes provision for the erection of loading platforms and the furnishing of cars at such platforms. Section 17 regulates the duties of grain commission merchants. Section 18 provides for the application of fees collected. Section 19 requires the officers mentioned in section 50 of the Manitoba Grain Act to make certain reports to the commisisoner. Section 20 provides penalties for infraction of the Act. Section 21 deals with the distribution of cars and makes provisions respecting the business of track buyers. Sections 22 and 23 deal with the question of storage charges.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: We had the assurance of my right hon. friend on Friday last and again on Wednesday that the proposed measure with regard to the transcontinental railway would be placed before the House not later than this week. Does my hon. friend propose to make any announcement to-day ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I trust that; my hon. friend's expectations will be fulfilled. The delays in bringing this measure before the House which has now been in session for about four and a half months, remind us very much of the delays in the celebrated case of Jarndyce vs. Jarudyce, and the House might regard itself in the position of Miss Flyte, who used to say she expected judgment on the Day of Judgment. My right hon. friend some times in days gone by has been discouraged about the progress of business, but I am sure on this side of the House we are getting discouraged in regard to the length of this session, and in connection with the delay to which the government persist in putting us day after day and week after week with regard to this matter. I definitely understood from my right hon. friend a week ago to-day, that that measure would be brought down this week. The right hon. gentleman then said it would be down probably early this week, but that it certainly would be down this week, and we are today as much in the dark as ever about it. Could not my right hon. friend at least give us an assurance as to a date beyond which he will not keep the House and the country waiting for this policy? He expects to be able to put it on the Order Paper to-day, but he does not pledge himself to do so, and we know that expectations are often disappointed. My right hon. friend's expectations with regard to this policy have been so often disappointed already that we really do not feel the same confidence in them with regard to this that we do with regard to some other matters. I would like, if my right hon. friend can do it-and I think the request is not an unreasonable one-that he should at least fix a date beyond which the House and the country will not be kept waiting for the announcement of this measure.

Well, Mr. Speaker, it is because expectations are often disappointed that I do not absolutely pledge myself to give the notice of motion to-day, although I think I shall be in a position to do so. My hon. friend is a lawyer, and he has reminded us of a celebrated case in which there was considerable delay. It is because I know something of the delays of lawyers that I do not absolutely pledge myself to give the notice which I expect to give. Unfortunately, I am in the hands of the lawyers at the present moment ; and, until they have completed their work, which I think they will do to-day, I cannot give that pledge. My hon. friend, being a member of the profession, knows that it would not do for me to pledge myself until I am absolutely sure that I shall be in a position to keep my word.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House in committee on the following resolution-The Minister of Finance.
That it is expedient to enact as follows :-
1. The Governor in Council may authorize the payment of a bounty to any corporation, firm or person manufacturing binder twine in Canada ; such bounty to be equal to the amount paid as export duty In the Philippine Islands, on manilla fibre produced in such islands, and used in the manufacture of binder twine in Canada. Such bounty shall only be payable in respect of binder twine manufactured on or after the first day of September, 1902. Provided, however. that the bounty shall not exceed three-eighths of one cent per pound, on the manilla fibre so used in the manufacture of binder twine.
3. The Governor in Council may make regulations .to carry out the intention of this Act.

At an earlier stage of the session I intimated that the government, while not willing to make any material change in the tariff in the present session, deeming that such a course would not be expedient, having regard to the general conditions of the country, might find it expedient to invite the attention of the House at a later stage to the condition of one or two industries in connection with some legislation touching the question of bounties. I mentioned at that time two particular industries, the manufacture of binder twine and the lead industry, and since that time we have introduced resolutions with regard to bounties on iron and steel. So that there are now on the notice paper three resolutions touching the question of bounties. The particular motion before us deals with the question of a bounty on binder twine. Binder twine is on our free list, and for some years the business has been carried on under that condition, and on the whole, I believe, has prospered. However, the industry has been placed at a

special disadvantage by certain United States legislation, not touching the question of import duties, but the question of export duties on the raw material which is produced in the Philippine Islands. About a year ago the United States government enacted a law under which, while an export duty of three-eighths of a cent per pound was levied on all manilla fibre exported from the Philippine Islands, and while all shippers of the material would have to pay that export duty, a special provision was made that if the material so exported from the Philippine Islands should be manufactured in the United States, and then shipped abroad, the shippers would get a rebate equivalent to the export duty. The net result is that while the manufacturer of binder twine in the United States has exemption from that duty, and can send the manufactured article into Canada free in competition with the product of our own manufacturers, the Canadian manufacturer, who imports his raw material also from the Philippine Islands, has to pay that export duty. In that way there is a substantial discrimination against the Canadian manufacturer of binder twine and in favour of the American manufacturer. It is not exactly a question of free trade. The Canadian manufacturer is placed in a much worse position than he could fie by the application of free trade principles. We have thought, therefore, that in order that we might compensate the manufacturer of Canada for that special and exceptional disadvantage under which he labours, we would provide for the payment of a bounty to the extent of the export duty. The bounty, of course, will only be paid on that portion of the manilla fibre which is imported into Canada and used in the manufacture of binder twine. Our statistics will easily show the quantity of manilla fibre imported into Canada from the Philippine Islands ; but as all that fibre is not used in the manufacture of binder twine, these statistics will not help us very much in estimating the amount that we shall have to pay under these resolutions. We propose that the bounty shall take effect on all binder twine manufactured in Canada from the 1st of September last. Our reason for fixing that date is that the law of the United States was passed upwards of a year ago, and the manufacture of all binder twine manufactured in Canada from manilla fibre for the present season began last autumn. We therefore propose that all binder twine manufactured in Canada from the 1st of September last shall be entitled to this bounty, on evidence being given that the manilla fibre which entered into its manufacture was imported directly or indirectly from the Philippine Islands and that the export duty was paid thereon. It is difficult to estimate what amount we shall have to pay under this item. It will not, however, toe a very large sum. The limitation is not as to the aggregate amount. It 2291
is as to the amount per pound of manilla fibre imported and used in the manufacture of binder twine.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Can the hon. minister inform me how many pounds of binder twine were imported into Canada from the United States last year, and the value of the same ; also, the quantity in pounds exported from Canada to the United States ? As I understand, there is an arrangement by which binder twine can be exported to the United States free of duty, though I believe there are some conditions in their law, the practical effect of which is to exclude our 'binder twine.

The total imports in 1902 were 14,927,302, I think practically all from the United States. The value of it was $1,507,344. Practically we have no exports to the United States. Binder twine under certain conditions is on the Americon free list. I think this refers to binder twine made of certain material which practically shuts out twine of our manufacture.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understand the hon. minister to say that under conditions that have existed during the past year the binder twine industry of Canada flourished?

For
several years-since the tariff was adopted.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Since binder twine was put on the free list?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I do not see how the hon. minister can say that when he tells us just now that we have imported nearly 1,500,000 pounds at a value of $1,507,000. This was all manufactured by American labour, and was sold to the Canadian farmer at higher prices than the farmer was able to buy it for before the binder twine was put on the free list. With a great flourish of trumpets the duty was taken off and some arrangement was announced to have been made under which it was said the Canadian manufacturer would have access to the markets of the United States. And to-day the minister admits that they made such conditions-and the figures prove it-that the Canadian manufacturer cannot export a pound of binder twine to the United States, though we import such a large quantity. Why does not the government protect the binder twine industry and establish this manufacture in Canada as it was before, so that Canadian labour may be employed and still the Canadian farmer get his binder twine cheaper than he can buy it today from the American trust? Instead of a vigorous policy of that kind the minister comes down and gives a little bounty, making it equivalent to what the Americans have, still leaving our market to the Americans, and gaining no chance for us to sell to them, putting about a million and a half

of Canadian money into the United States, a great portion of which is paid for labour, and leaving our farmers still subject to the extortion of trust prices for their binder twine. I understand that our binder twine factories have been practically closed for the last two or three years. They have been before the government asking for relief and this is the relief they7 are given.

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) perhaps, is not aware that, during the last couple of years the Canadian manufacturers of binder twine have been able to carry on operations only by the favour of their American rivals. I make this statement because I have undoubted evidence that it is true. The American manufacturers of binder twine came over to this country and told the Canadian manufacturers :	Unless you
limit your product, we will slaughter the market, and you will not. be allowed to manufacture at all. If the Minister of Finance wishes to hold an inquiry into the case, he will find that every word of my statement is true. Under these circumstances, the minister has no right to say that the manufacture of binder twine in Canada is prospering. I say it again: The American manufacturers told the Canadian manufacturers that unless they limited their product they would be slaughtered

Mr. CLARIvE. The Americans fixed the price.	-

Of course. We are practically in the hands of the American trust. That is an unfair position. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance says he proposes this bounty on account of special circumstances in the binder twine industry, as it is protected in the United States. But he has no right to take that stand, in my humble opinion ; because while he invokes that pretext in his action in regard to binder twine, he intends also to ask parliament to give bounties in the case of lead and in the case of iron and steel, though these special circumstances do not exist in these industries in the United States. The principle we are asked to sanction to-day is not a fair principle. We are asked to take out of the pockets of the tax-payers of this country large sums of money to pay to the manufacturers of binder twine in Canada. If, instead of this, we had a protective policy, a straight Canadian policy, the taxpayer would not be called upon to contribute money to individuals or to firms.
And the farmers would get that binder twine cheaper.

Yes, because, as I said, we are practically in the hands of the American trust to-day and have been for a year or more. Of course, I speak independently, for I am responsible for the very policy that has been followed. I do not say that it had my approval-very far from it. i Mr. TAYLOR.
But I remained a member of the government while that policy was adopted and carried out. I am fully responsible. So, I do not speak in a party spirit at all. Not by any means. But I say again that the principle we are asked to sanction to-day is not a proper remedy. It is unfair to the tax-payer ; and it will not inspire confidence among the manufacturers or induce them to invest more capital in this industry. It is, as I said on another occasion, an expedient ; and expedients have never, to my knowledge, produced permanent good results. However, those of us who do not share the views of the Minister of Finance and his colleagues are obliged to accept the remedy that is offered. We cannot get everything we want; we are bound to accept what we can get.

The House and the country will hear with great regret the announcement of the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) here to-day. In substance he has told us that the efforts of the government in the direction of the revision of the tariff and increased protection have no results, but the granting of bounty on iron and steel, on lead and on binder twine. I have been studying the question rather closely of late, anil watching the signs of the times on the other side of the boundray line. If there is anything in view at the present day, it is that we have in America reached ' the crest of the wave, ' as the Minister of Finance called it some time ago. The people of the United States, as a nation and a manufacturing nation, are preparing themselves to make a slaughter house of Canada. I believe that the present financial disturbance on the other side of the line is merely precursory of a movement which is spreading all over the union which seeks wider markets, and I believe that before the day is out we shall hear something of a movement that has been inaugurated in the North-western states, with its centre in Minneapolis, which looks forward to some arrangement as a result of the coming meeting of the commission which will increase the markets of the Americans at the expense of Canadians. I believe that that movement is widespread, and that every effort will be made, when the commission meets, to break down the barriers we have and turn the Canadian market over to the American manufacturer. I believe the country views this with alarm, which will not be made less by the policy announced by the Finance Minister, limiting the action of the government to the granting of bounties to the extent he has named. If there ever was a time when we should have an up-and-up, forward protectionist policy it is to-day. We propose to go into extensive expenditure on railways in this country ; we propose to grant millions and millions of money to build railways : and yet we have not the courage in this House, and this government has not

tlie courage, to adopt a protectionist policy with regard to steel and iron. If that were the case we would have rolling mills established in this country to build all these railways, we would have, as we are likely to have, the Steel Association of the United States coming over into this country-but I am not quite sure that is the case. But we do know this, that the prospects of reciprocal trade relations between the mother country and Canada have already compelled a large number of American concerns to consider the advisability of locating their export trade arrangements in Canada. We know what has happened in the town of Peterborough. A large cereal company in the United States saw what was coming, and they organized to do all their export business from Canada, and are now establishing large works in this country. So with the steel industry, with a vigorous protectionist policy to bring it about. It is being brought about now in England because they are becoming protectionists there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are not discussing the general question of the tariff.
But the Finance Minister opened up the whole question, and that is my excuse.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Because the Finance Minister or some other minister has opened up an irrelevant matter, that does not make it in order. The question before us is the propriety of giving a bounty on the manufacture of binder twine. Under this resolution we cannot discuss the general tariff.
ilr. BORDEN (Halifax). But the hon. gentleman is perfectly in order, in criticising this resolution, to show to the House that a protective tariff would be a better protection.

I did not open up the whole question of steel, though I have no objection, if the Chairman will permit us to do so, to these three resolutions all being considered at once, if any body desires to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Notwithstanding the minister's statement, I am here to see that the discussions are in order, and I say that the tariff is not now the subject before the Chair. It is entirely out of order to discuss the propriety of giving a duty on other things. Unless the committee will decide to discuss the general question of the tariff, then I must keep the committee within reasonable bounds.

I think the Minister of Finance has raised the general question of the tariff by proposing a bounty. We are raising the question that duties by customs can be levied more advantageously to the commerce of the country. I think, I am in order, when the issue of protection and
free trade is raised as it has been, to refer to the general issue, and on that line, unless you interfere with me, 1 propose to continue for a few moments. My statement is that if we had had due protection in this country, not spasmodic protection like this, we would have a new era of prosperity. We would be in a position to take care of ourselves now when this threatened invasion of our territory is likely to take place. For the Americans see that we are not genuine in our protectionist views, because we know, as has been stated here to-day, that our liberty in respect to binder twine is controlled by an American trust. There are other industries that have been ignored in this country. I refer to the ship-building industry. A bounty might very well be given to the steel ship-building industry. I believe the case that has been put forward in favour of a bounty in connection with ship-building in this country is unanswerable. The hon. gentleman must have had the papers presented to him. I have seen some of them, and so far as I can gather from these papers, the time has come when a bounty ought to be applied to the steel ship-building industry of Canada, and foreign built ships ought to be excluded from the coasting trade of Canada. All we are told here to-day is that we are to have bounties on iron and steel and on lead and on binder twine. The fact is that there are a great many industries that ought to be taken up and ought to have protection applied to them in order that we may be able to meet the threatened American invasion, and get the benefit of keeping our work for our own workingmen and our own market for our own products. That time seems to be near at hand. There is another instance which I wish to mention, and that is the market gardeners of this country. Their market has been given over entirely, for all kinds of early fruit and vegetables, to the Americans. They have petitioned us from time to time for some kind of protection. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would apply the bounty principle to them. But so far the hon. gentleman has given them no encouragement, and their market is departing from them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must insist upon the hon. gentleman keeping to the question. I am going to make this a test, and if the committee do not stand by me, they will have to appeal to the House in the matter. My decision is this, that the speakers must confine tlieir remarks to the question before the Chair. We cannot wander away to steel, and market gardens, and a hundred questions besides. My decision is that the discussion must be limited to the propriety of this parliament granting a bounty on the manufacture of twine in Canada.
I am discussing the bounty question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The bounty is applicable to one hundred and forty questions. We are now discussing the propriety of giving a bounty to a certain industry.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is it not perfectly proper for the hon. gentleman, in criticising this resolution, to point out to the House that it is not wide enough ? I do not regard that as beyond the bounds of criticism. The hon. gentleman finds a resolution here which proposes to give a bounty to the manufacturers of binder twine ; is he not perfectly in order in pointing out that the resolution should not stop there, but should extend to various other things, which in his opinion, should receive encouragement by way of bounty ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot understand how it could be argued in considering this question, that a bounty should be given to market gardeners because they raise cabbages and other vegetables, I cannot see the relevancy at all. I do not see the relevancy of the question of giving a bounty to every industry in the country to the special question that is before the Chair.
Is it not in order to discuss the principle of bounty ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No.
Well, that is narrowing it down to a very small limit.
Might I ask if we could put the member for East York (Mr. Maclean) in order by moving that the committee rise ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No.
Can we not move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again ? May I ask your ruling on that point ?

Upon such a motion as that we could not depart from the subject under discussion, the discussion would have to be strictly confined to the subject in hand. Therefore the hon. gentleman would not help us by moving that the committee rise in order to give the floor to another member. For myself, if I may assume the role of a peacemaker, although we are transgressing to some extent the rules of the House, I would be willing to allow my hon. friend from East York to speak upon the tariff question, wrhich he has so miicli at heart. Though I think he is in the wrong, I would be quite willing to allow him to expound his views.
Mr. ROCHE iHalifax). In regard to this subject of bounty
Mr. Chairman, then with your indulgence, I will put it that way

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Am I to understand that the committee is satisfied with the present range of the discussion ?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Because' if the committee is satisfied, then the responsibility is taken off my shoulders and I lose control of the committee.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If I raise a point of order, I am either right or wrong. If I am wrong, I will apologize to the committee, if I am right, then I want to retain control of the committee so that I may guide it in the discussion. The way to ascertain the ruling of the House is not to move that the committee rise, but simply to say :	I appeal to the House for their
decision.
No, no, that is not the way at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I beg your pardon, but, however, as that question is not before us, I do not suppose it is necessary to discuss it.

It is not an uncommon thing by the general consent of the House to allow the discussion to be broadened. I am sure every member of the House on both sides desires to uphold the Chair, and we are quite satisfied that the chairman is only desirous of maintaining the rules of the House, but it is a general practice by common consent to allow the discussion to be broadened and my own opinion wrould be that the chairman should not keep us too closely to the question. There are two or three resolutions on the Oraer paper dealing with the same class of subjects and I would rather that we had liberty to refer to them, but when we do exercise that liberty we must not hold the chairman responsible for establishing a precedent which will prevent the committee at another time from keeping closely to the rule.

I think the hon. gentleman (Air. Maclean) is perfeptly in order. He is discussing the question in reference to binder twine and surely you may say that if you are going to grant a bounty on binder twine it is necessary that a similar concession should be given in regard to other articles. I have been a long time in the House and I have never heard such an interpretation given the rule as that which has been given by the chairman of the committee. Every one in the House, I am sure, desires that the dignity of the House and that the rules of order shall be preserved and especially that the ruling of the chairman shall be accepted when he is correct. But, I beg to differ from the chairman and I wish to stick strictly to the rules. He has no right to appeal to the committee. If his ruling is wrong our duty is to put it in writing, appeal to the House, call in the Speaker and have his opinion upon the

subject and if necessary appeal from the ruling of the Speaker to the House.

That is exact-lj the position X took. I thought I was right then and I am of the same opinion still. It is the duty of any person who does not believe I am right in my ruling to appeal to the House. I would rather that an hon. member would do that than that I should sit here knowing that I am perfectly right in regard to my ruling and have it disregarded. Almost every time I have ruled in the committee in an effort to keep the committee to their work and to facilitate the despatch of business I have been overruled by one party or the other. The result is that the session is extended week after week and I am kept sitting here without any progress being made in the business. When I give a ruling that in the opinion of the committee is not according to the rule then I would like to have the opinion of the House upon the matter and then I will know whether I am right or not and will not be obliged to submit to the lectures of parties who think I am wrong when as a matter of fact I am perfectly satisfied I am right as I believe I am now. However, the responsibility will be upon the committee.

There is a rule which means something or it does not mean anything. If there is a rule that requires hon. members to stick to the subject under discussion then, certainly, that rule should be enforced. If the remarks of my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) are pertinent to the subject under discussion, then any member of this House can say anything he likes on any subject when any question comes before the House.
No, no.
Certainly.
Protection or bounty.

Certainly he may say anything on any subject. It is quite evident that unless the rules are to be supported, we cannot carry on business. Of course, the chairman cannot dictate to individual members under the privilege of parliament as to what they shall say if these members are supported by other members, but unless members of this House are prepared to support the chairman in rulings that are according to common sense as well as according to the rule of the House we certainly cannot do business with very much credit to the country or to ourselves.

I do not think that the hon. member for Axoerta (Mr. Oliver) has stated the case fairly. The hon. Minister of Finance came forward here with a proposition to grant bounties. I have not departed from that in the least and I intend to stick most closely to the subject.
Binder twine.

The question of bounties having been introduced I am discussing the desirability of extending these bounties to other things. I think the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and ine right hon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir AVilfrid Laurier) agree that I am within the rule. I propose to show why a bounty system should be applied to the ship-building industries of Canada as well as to binder twine and for this purpose I shall read a short communication setting out the arguments in favour of my contention.
Certain of the component parts of a ship not manufactured in Canada-but imported either from Great Britain or the United States are subject to duty. Certain other of the component parts of a ship manufactured in Canada upon which duty is not directly paid but by reason of our tariff the price includes if not the whole at least nearly the same duty as if imported. The coal used in the construction of a ship is subject to duty. Nearly the whole of the material used in the construction of a ship has to be imported either from the United States or Great Britain ; during the .last eighteen mouths almost exclusively from Great Britain, because satisfactory delivery could not be obtained in the United States. The freight and marine insurance on this material amount to considerable. The carpets and furnishings throughout pay duty directly if imported. If not imported indirectly on account of our tariff. The difference in labour is also very considerable. the wages paid in this country being fully fifteen per cent higher than in Great Britain. This difference, however, I am glad to say "would be somewhat lessened, because I believe men in this country perform more work per hour than they do in Great Britain.
In Great Britain, coal and structural material are in close proximity to the shipyards, and therefore are obtained at a minimum of cost. All parts of a ship including its furnishings are obtainable on the lowest basis of cost of production on account of the tariff of Great Brit!lOur chief competitor for the building of new ships is Great Britain, and while Canadian shipbuilding is subject to the several disadvantages above mentioned, amounting to rather more than $4 per gross registered ton, British built ships are permitted to come into Canada entirely free of duty, and are afforded the same privileges in Canada as Canadian built ships. This we do not at all object to, as Canadian built ships are afforded the same freedom in all British ports, but what we desire is that the government consider the advisability of affording such 'a rebate or bounty as will be equal to the disabilities under which we labour, amounting as stated to rather more than $4 per gross registered ton, and thus place the ship-building industry in Canada on a parity with the same industry in Great Britain. This being done I feel sure there will be no more newiy built British ships brought into Canada, but that they will be built in Canada, as they can be obtained at no more cost than if built in Great Britain, and will be more suitable at least for the lake traffic.
In the days of wooden ship-building in Canada it was considered fair to allow a rebate of $1.15 per net registered ton on the highest class of

steel-kneed vessels built in this country. Thus it will be seen that what we are now seeking was recognized years ago to the extent then required.
Then suitable wood for the construction of vessels could be conveniently had in Canada. Now scarcely any wooden ships are being built, but steel ships are taking their place, and instead of being able to obtain the material convenient to the shipyards as was the case when wood was used, the material has to be imported, as already stated.
In addition to this required subsidy of $4 per gross registered ton, it is earnestly desired that foreign built ships be excluded entirely from Canadian coasting privileges, the same as Canadian built ships are excluded from coasting privileges in foreign countries, and that foreign built ships be not admitted to coasting privileges at any rate of duty unless and until Canadian ships are admitted subject to the same rate of duty or license fee as is now charged in Canada.
The gentlemen who drew up that paper made out a case which they presented to the government some time ago which, I think, justified the extension of this principle of bounties to the production of steel ships in Canada. If it were applied to the production of steel ships in Canada we would have large shipyards all over the country. I believe that we have the ore, we have the coal and we have everything necessary for the production of steel ships, but tbe encouragement which applied protection would give them in the shape of a bounty. I think it Is time that the government had the courage of their convictions. They have not the courage of their convictions'; that is the trouble. They believe in protection but they will not live up to it. They have been converted to it and they carry out the principle at times In a spasmodic way, but if they would carry it out in its entirety in these growing times, when Canada is going ahead, when we propose to spend millions on our railways and give some encouragement to the steel ship-building industry we would have immense shipyards in the country and we would be building the ships that would run in connection with the transcontinental roads from, their ports on the upper lakes. We would he following the example of the United States which stands to-day in the first position.
In regard to ship-building ?

No, hut in regard to a great many things and the great danger to this country to-day is that it is 'threatened with an invasion of the products of the American manufacturers who attained to a position to rival Canadian manufacturers and drive them out of their own market by the thorough adoption of the principle of protection. I disagree somewhat with the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) who said that the system of bounties was not a good form of protection. In a great many cases the bounty Is the highest form of the protective system. It is sometimes the most efficacious

form of protection and I would like to see it applied in other directions. I not only hope to see the government extend that policy to steel ship-building, to lead, to binder twine and to steel and iron, but I would like to see it extended to a great many other things, and I would like to see the customs employed so as to increase the measure of protection that the manufacturers and workmen of this country ought to have. I have been led, as I said to the committee a short time ago, to make these remarks by reason of what is transpiring in the United States to-day. I almost fear that a financial crash of some kind is impending over there. The manufacturers are making money, the railway companies! are making money, and yet, by reason of something that lias happened there, they see their markets threatened, they have more production than they know what to do with and they are preparing to make a slaughter market of Canada as they did in the old days, but, if this government had the courage of their convictions and if they had the courage to put the protective principle into force they would give us bounties on all these things as well as customs duties so as to give increased protection to Canadian workmen and Canadian manufacturers.

I have to apologize for appearing to again rise, when a question of order was being decided by chair, but I regret to say that from this part of the House it is impossible to tell what is being said. Hon. gentlemen speaking from the lower benches upon this side of the House have their hacks turned towards us, and it is very rare that we are able to catch one word in ten that is said. We sometimes hear lion, gentlemen on the front row of the other side of the House, as there is a better opportunity of the sound being carried across. Hon. 'gentlemen speaking at the back of the chamber on the other side cannot be heard on this side without very great difficulty. With regard to the question of bounty on hinder twine, I would ask gentlemen opposite what better device could be adopted to enable our manufacturers of hinder twiue in this country to make it here than the one now proposed. The United States and Spain unfortunately went to war: the United States was the victor and they took possession of the territory where the raw material for the manufacture of binder twine grows. If we attempted to prohibit the importation of American binder twine into this country, it is possible that the United States government might retaliate by refusing to allow any of the raw material to he sold to Canada. There is a monopoly in New York at the present time for the purpose of controlling the trade altogether, and I believe that the bounty now proposed is the only possible way of aiding the manufacturers in tliis country. If we attempt'd

to slnit out American twine there might be a reprisal in the shape of a refusal to give us the raw material, and then we would be at the mercy of the American twine manufacturers altogether.
What is the export duty imposed on the raw material by the United States ?
Three-eights of a cent, I understand.
What was the average price paid by our farmers for binder twine last year ?
I do not know what the farmers paid in the west exactly, but I know that the price has been falling steadily.

Is it the argument of the hon. gentleman that in order to placate those who control the production of the raw material, the people of Canada generally should have to pay this duty of three-eighths of a cent a pound ?
What I say is that it is better to assist the industry by a bounty, under the circumstances, than by placing a higher duty on the manufactured article.
I understand from the hon. gentleman's argument that we are practically living on sufferance in this country ?
So we are.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) would place us in a very humiliating position. If the advice of the member for East York (Mr. Maclean) were accepted, and if a duty was placed on binder twine which would protect our own manufacturers and keep them fully employed, the result would be far better, and our farmers, instead of paying 12 to 14 cents a pound for binder twine, would be paying 10 cents.
What would the hon. gentleman do suppose we were prohibited altogether from getting the raw material out of which binder twine is made?
I would be prepared to answer that question when the prohibition was put on. The hon. gentleman is simply imagining a fallacious argument to justify him in supporting the resolution.
I can assure the hon. gentleman that it is a positive fact.

The contention of the hon. member (Mr. Roche is well worthy of consideration. Our dealings with the United States teach us that the United States are looking after the United States all the time. If I am right in the contention that we cannot get the raw material except through the United States, then we are in the hands ol' the United States to
that 'extent. Our experience would lead us to believe that if we built up a tariff wall which wrould shut out any of their manufactures we might reasonably expect that they would build up such a wall as would prevent us getting the raw material, and so prevent us altogether from making binder twine in this country.
What would be the effect of putting a bounty on the production of lead in Canada?

The difference is that we have the raw material for the manufacture of lead in Canada, and that we have not the raw material for the making of binder twine. It is absolutely necessary that our farmers should have binder twine and if we cannot get the raw material otherwise than through the United States, will any gentleman say that we are not in their hands to that extent?

The fallacious reasoning of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) is that because manilla comes to us through the United States we must avoid building up our binder twine industry in Canada by bounty and a duty for fear we would offend the Americans. Does he think that any nation would be so small as to prevent us giving a bounty to our manufacturers to the extent that they allow a rebate to the manufacturers on the raw material that comes from the Philippine Islands ?
i was talking about a duty and not a bounty.
It amounts to the same thing.
Not at all.

When manilla is exported to any other country but the United States there is an export duty on it, and the Canadian government propose to reimburse the manufacturers in Canada to the extent of that export duty, thus putting the Canadian manufacturer on the same level as the American manufacturer in respect to the raw material.
To that I agree.

Yes, but that at best is only a half-way measure, because while we reimburse the Canadian manufacturer to the extent of the export duty, we still allow the Americans to throw their twine into Canada. I want to have the Canadian market for the Canadian manufacturer, and if we did justice to the Canadian manufacturer we would not only compensate him to the extent of the export duty on the raw material, but we would go further and put a duty upon binder twine coming into Canada to secure for him the Canadian market. Is that wrong or is it right ?

I am not saying that it is wrong or that it is right, but if we are compelled to get our raw material through the United States, and if we shut

out American binder twine, does not the hon. gentleman think it possible that we might be prevented from getting raw material altogether ?

I do not think anything of the kind, because if that prohibition were applied to Canada it would have to be applied to the rest of the world, and no nation would dare to do that. Are we to be forever cringing to the United States or to any other country in respect to our trade. Are we to be afraid to build up any industry in this country because it may offend the United States that we should do so. I have heard that argument so often from the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) in past years that I am sick of it. We are not worthy of being Britons if we are not above such an argument as that. Let us do what is in the interest if our own people without regarding what any other country may think or do.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) say that the member for North Norfolk has advocated submitting to unjust demands on the part of the American people or surrendering our rights in any respect in our negotiations with them ? Is that the charge the hon. gentleman makes ?

I have heard the hon. member for North Norfolk use this argument when dealing with this subject. When a proposal was made to put an export duty on logs so as to insure the manufacture of our lumber at home, and I was advocating it, I was told by the hon. member :	" Beware, or you will exasperate the United States; they could stop commercial intercourse with us at any time, and they will do it if you go too far; you will only worry and annoy them. Don't we know that they could hinder us in many ways ? They could stop the bonding privilege that we enjoy and all commercial intercourse with us.' I refer to that because I have heard it so often, and his argument now is exactly on the same line. When in the interests of Canada we propose to do something, are we always to be told :	Don't let us do it,
because they will strike back ? They are so small a people in their national aspirations that they w'ould do it if we dared to do something in the interests of Canada. I do not think that is an argument that should ever be used in this Canadian parliament. I have always thought that as a nation we should do what the interests of this country require, regardless of any other nation, precisely as they do in the United States. They put on or take off a duty just as it suits the interests of their own people, and they do not consider whether it restricts the trade of England, Canada, Germany, or any other country. I say that the interests of our country to-day require that we should not only give this bounty, and thereby remove a handicap which our Mr. GALLIHER.
manufacturers are labouring under owing to the regulations made by the United States government, but that for the purpose of keeping our market for our Canadian manufactures, we should go further and put a duty on all binder twine coming into this country from any other country. If we did that, w*e believe the twine would not be increased in price to the consumer here, but we would build up the manufacture in Canada to such an extent that competition would bring down the price to the lowest possible figure to the Canadian consumer, as it did before, and we would have binder twine at its real worth; whereas to-day we are obliged to take it from the United States, whether the price is high or low.
I desire to say one word, as I have been alluded to by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I am afraid that this discussion is getting a little beyond the bounds.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ruled that some time ago, but the committee took it out of my hands, so that they are responsible for it.

I am not taking the initiative, but desire very briefly to reply to the hon. gentleman's allusion to myself. The statements made with regard to the necessity of embarking upon tariff legislation, and the criticisms made upon the conduct of the government because they are not disposed to go so far as our friends in the opposition think is proper, are in my opinion entirely uncalled for, inappropriate and out of season. We have had the statement made by the government that in consequence of certain conditions, it was not deemed proper to open the tariff question this session; and I for one supported that position entirely irrespective of any abstract or practical views I might entertain upon the question of tariff legislation. The ground taken by the government was that as negotiations of a most important character are pending, the outcome of which will create conditions that will require action in one direction or another-negotiations the outcome of which we cannot foresee, and in consequence of which we cannot predicate our action in tariff matters upon known conditions-the government would abstain from tariff legislation this session, and would wait until it knew definitely and could move intelligently in the course which it would be proper for it to take. I endorsed that position. I would endorse that position as a protectionist. I would endorse it as a member of this House governed by practical considerations. The government, notwithstanding that position, proceeds to the extent which is necessary in the public interest, to relieve certain interests in Canada which are suffering from causes which the government may be able to remove. To that extent the government are justified in moving in this matter, and

they can do it with perfect consistency with the* position they have taken. Beyond that I do not think it would be proper for the government to go. So far I would support them; beyond that I would not. With regard to the charge which the hon. member has made with reference to myself, it has been a very usual thing for more than a quarter of a century to answer anything I may have said in this House by the statement that I was a Yankee. That has always been considered a sufficient answer to set aside any argument or statement 1 might advance.
I may remind the hon. gentleman that I uttered no word about his being a Yankee.

I did not say the hon. gentleman did; I am talking about the general course pursued. The hon. gentleman says to-day that 1 have in the past advocated the adoption of policies dictated by fear of retaliation by the Americans. The inference is that in doing so I have shown a craven spirit and a desire to bow to the Americans; and when asked for some specific case, the hon. gentleman brings up the old question of the export duty on logs. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have consistently, during all the years that that question has been under discussion in this House, opposed an export duty. I have opposed an export duty on anything, I do not care what it is. We are to-day, in the resolutions under discussion, meeting the question of an export duty unfairly imposed by another country for the purpose of injuring one of our interests. X condemn that export duty as being wrong. X condemn export duties in all cases as being wrong in principle. I have condemned them on every occasion in the past, and I will condemn them in the future, and in doing this, I am not showing any craven spirit or bowing to dictation from a foreign country, but merely contending for justice and fair play. I condemned the proposal to put an export duty on logs in our own country. I did that because the owner of standing pine would have its value reduced to the extent of the export duty for the benefit of the sawmill interest in the country. The friends of the sawmill interest advocated the imposition of an export duty for the benefit of that interest and to the' detriment of the standing pine owner, and its imposition was essentially unjust, bad politics, and bad political economy. I opposed that export duty on broad public principles, and I wish to say to the hon. gentleman that his insinuation with regard to the course I pursue in this matter is unfair and unworthy of him. I have stood up in this House during the thirty-one years that I have had a seat here and advocated what I believed to be Canadian interests on the broad ground of the benefit of Canada, and I have had no motive or impulse beyond this during all that time. I have done this
often in the face of opposition and prejudice, and have incurred on many occasions charges of the most unfriendly, unwarrantable and untruthful character. I stand here to say I have never been in favour of surrendering a single Canadian right. I will go as far as any man in this House or in this country in maintaining Canadian rights, and I only await the proper hour when circumstances and developments show us the proper course to pursue, in order to follow the dictates of my convictions.

The hon. member who has just taken his seat says that the opposition proposed more than the government now propose for the binder twine industry. I wish to ask him if he thinks the government are going as far as they should go to protect that industry V Mr. CHARLTON. I do not know that that has anything to do with the question. The government are introducing a resolution granting a bounty in order to counteract an unfair discrimination in the form of an export duty which has been imposed in favour of the United States; and in doing that are only doing justice to our own manufactures.
I think it is only reasonable to ask the hon. gentleman if he thinks the proposal they have made is as far as they should go in the interest of the binder twine industry ?

I have only to say, as I said before, that the question of dealing with the tariff on broad principles, on the principles of protection versus free trade, is lying in abeyance, awaiting certain developments and the conclusion of certain negotiations. In the meantime, the government proposes in this resolution, not upon protective principles or non-proteetive principles, to remove the disability of an unfair discrimination that now interferes with a manufacturing interest in Canada.
What are we waiting for now before proceeding to the consideration of the revision of the tariff ?
We want to know whether we are to engage in a commercial war. or whether we are to have peace.

We have another significant announcement. First, we have the Minister of Finance saying that only three interests were to be considered. Now, a supporter of his gets up and gives us the reasons. That reason is that we are to go into negotiations with the United States, they to have the big end of the stick and we to have the little end. If we went into the negotiations having a tariff like their own, we should be able to accomplish something. The hon. gentleman says ; Do not put up the tariff now, but go to the Americans with your low tariff and make a reciprocal arrangement with them, giving them the Can-

adian market. Why, that is where hon. gentlemen opposite have always made their mistake. They should have met the Americans with tariff for tariff, and then they would be in a position to negotiate with them and maintain Canadian rights. It is the old story of ' looking to Washington.' Evidently these hon. gentlemen are going to Washington and going with their hands tied. That is not the way to tight the Americans. We should stand up to them like men ; meet them with a tariff equal to their own, impose that tariff in the interest of Canada, and make it a thoroughly protectionist tariff so as to keep our markets for ourselves.

The subject we are now discussing would have interested me a great deal at the time of the budget debate. But the government, for reasons that were quite clear to themselves, decided not to open this question of the duty on binder twine. I am convinced that the manufacture of binder twine, like every other industry in this country, should have its interests looked after by the government, and should not have been singled out as the only industry subjected to competition from the other side. That question was discussed at the time of the budget debate. But to reopen it now will not answer any good purpose.
Who is opening it ?
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) mean unfair competition through the export duty of the United States, or through the withdrawal of the protective tariff in Canada ?

On general principles, I said, binder twine should receive the same measure of protection granted to every other industry. And I said it was not right that it should be singled out and deprived of the benefits of what we call our revenue tariff.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) to say that this is the only industry singled out in this way 7
This and barbed wire.
Well name the other as well as this.

This is the one we are talking about. The barbed wire industry is small and very little capital was injured by putting barbed wire on the free list.
At the time, there were not many binder twine manufactories in Canada. Most of them have come into existence since. The $7.50 per ton proposed by this Bill is to compensate the manufacturers for this $0.82 bonus that the United States manufacturer gets. In so far as this bounty will be of service to the manufacturers of binder twine in this country, I am glad the government are going to give it. I should have been glad personally if they had given 12J per cent protection. All these arguments of my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) that the United States might prohibit the exportation of manilla fabric to any other part of the world but the United States, do not appear to have any effect upon the owners of Canadian binder twine factories, the men who have their money invested in this business ; for tliev have ail petitioned in favour of a tariff protection of 12J per cent. So, I do not think there is much in those arguments. The fact that confronts me is that the government have decided, after a discussion, not to open the question of a duty on binder twine. When that question once more presents itself, I shall do what I did before-urge them both privately and in the House to put on a duty. They did not listen to that plea before, and now it is too late to discuss the question. I can assure them of my sincere desire that this Bill should become law ; because, to the extent that it compensates the manufacturers of binder twine for the unfair competition to which they are subjected, it is certainly of benefit to that industry. On pure manilla, 650-foot twine, there will be the full benefit of -} cents per pound. On 600-foot twine which contains about 60 per cent of manilla, there will be a proportionate benefit, and so on through the various qualities down to the lowest on which there will be little benefit to the manufacturer. This is not so much as I would like to see. But. to get up a general discussion on this particular item is going a little far afield.
I think. And when you, Mr. Chairman, find fault with the committee for overriding your decision I venture to say that it is only because you do not put your foot down and insist on those decisions being observed. For my part, I was prepared to endorse and uphold your decision that this general question should not be discussed on the motion before the committee.
Mr. JOHNSTON (Cardwell) I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) a question. He says he is in favour of a high protective tariff on binder twine. Did lie vote for high protection on binder twine or did he vote against it ?

Mr: HBYD. I do not know that there was a resolution moved on the subject of placing a duty on binder twine. But if there had been, and if I had played to the galleries by recording my single vote on this side in favour of such a resolution, my action would have been regarded as insincere by hou. gentlemen opposite. If the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in some way or other involved the idea of putting a duty on binder twine, I can only say that I voted in favour of the government's contention on that occasion.
And the resolution was in favour of adequate protection?
But ' adequate protection,' in my opinion is a very inadequate phrase.

In the discussion before us to-day we have primarily a matter of fact. We have left that and drifted into matters of sentiment and imagination. The matter of fact before us is f cents per pound on manilla. The object of this is to put our manufacturers of binder twine in as favourable a position as that they formerly occupied. But the discussion has drifted off to the matter of higher protection. I hare waited for some time to find out on what basis of protection the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) wotild wish us to go. And he has stated that his basis of protection would be the same as that of the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte), the adoption of a tariff equal to the American tariff. Now, suppose we put the tariff on binder twine up to 45 per cent. It is a matter of belief on my part that that would raise the price of binder twine to the consumer
What was the experience?
I think it was the same thing.

Perhaps the hou. gentleman will allow me to say that I never said here or elsewhere, that it would be necessary to have the same tariff on all articles that the Americans have. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Schell) will not find that in my speeches anywhere.
' Tariff for tariff ' was the word throughout the budget debate. And my hon. friend from East York has just now stated that that is what he would propose.
Hear, hear.

If we were to apply the American tariff to this importation of 15,000,000 pounds of binder twine, that would mean a tax upon the people of this country of $487,000, say half a million dollars, upon this article alone.
But if we did not import the binder twine, we would not pay the duty.
The quantities of twine imported were about 15,000,000 pounds, and if the tariff were in force which these gentlemen advocate
Does not the hou. gentleman claim that if we imposed a tariff of 40 per cent it would raise the price 40 per cent ?

It would give them an opportunity to do it if they wished, and there are very few people in business, regardless of their politics, who do not take advantage of the opportunity. That is the experience, not only in Canada, but everywhere else, because it is human nature. If you give them the opportunity they will take advantage of it; and it is idle to talk to farmers, at all events, or to myself, and to say that if you put up the duty to 45 per cent
May I ask the hon. gentleman this question ? When the duty of 12)c. per pound was taken off, did it lower the price of twine ?

The hon. gentleman may answer that question himself, I claim that it did. The question before us is this, Are we now to put on a duty of 45 per cent and raise the value of the twine manufactured in Canada, on the basis of the 15,000,000 pounds, to the extent of half a million dollars, or should we put on a bounty of three-eighths of a cent per pound, which amounts to $56,250 upon that 15,000,000 pounds imported ? This three-eighths of a cent is a very small trifle, as the hon. member for East York says, ' a miserable thing.' But if it puts the manufacturers in Canada to-day upon an equal basis with the Americans, where they have been for the last six or seven years, surely that should not be called a miserable thing. The manufacture of binder twine in Canada has been a profitable 'venture for those who have been engaged in it, with one exception, and I wish to draw attention to that exception. Under the old regime it will be remembered that practically every binder twine factory in the Dominion of Canada went into the hands of an American trust, ;every one, I believe, but one. They were all bought up by an American trust, and the binder twine manufacture of Canada to-day is largely in the hands of Americans, the largest amount of capital.
Was the Central Prison factory bought up, and the Kingston Penitentiary ?
These were not manufacturing concerns.
And the Brantford manufactory ?
Yes, that was bought up by the Americans.
Well, I have in my hands here to-day letters from farmers who were owners of this factory, and consumers-

I wish to state to the hon. member for St. Mary's that he is entirely wrong. The Brantford factory was bought up by Americans, and immediately after that was bought up the farmers' binder twine factory was started, and that farmers' binder twine factory was then the only independent factory in Canada, and In three years they declared a dividend to the extent of 250 per cent upon their stock. But it was not until after the Liberal government came into power, and allowed them to make these profits, when they were manufacturing without any duty.
They went into the trust.

No, that was when they were an independent concern. But we are drifting away from the question. The question before us is this, shall the farmers in this country, on 15,000,000 pounds of binder twine, be taxed a sum of $500,000 ; or, as proposed by the Minister of Finance, shall the manufacturers of this country be given a compensation for the injury inflicted upon them by the United States, of $56,250 7 That is a question we are discussing. brought down to actual figures. I am willing to vote in favour of the farmer paying no more than $56,000, instead of paying $500,000.

Perhaps the Finance Minister could tell us, in the absence of the Minister of Customs, on the basis of the imports for the last fiscal year, what will be the charge on the consolidated fund imposed by this bounty for the present fiscal year ?

That is difficult to tell, because our imports are not entirely confined to manufacturers of binder twine ; twine is largely used for other purposes, for general cordage. But I would think that probably it would be $25,000 to $50,000, possibly more. I have some hesitation in giving an estimate, but I do not think it would exceed $50,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) and the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) have, if I understood them rightly, both expressed themselves in favour of giving a bounty rather than an increased duty. Now, I presume both these 'hon. gentlemen represent largely workingmen. The Minister of Finance, in reply to my bon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke), has stated that a very large sum of money will have to be taken qut of the taxes paid ,jy the people generally to make up this bounty. Now. I want to ask these hon. gentlemen what right the workingmen of Canada have to pay taxes in order to lower the price of binder twine Mr. SCHELL.
to the farmers?-because it will have that effect. If you put on a duty, the party using the article pays the duty; the consumer pays the duty, there is no question about that. But if you put on enough duty, there would be no importation. The people in the North-west can raise all the flax we require to make our own binder twine. If the Minister of Finance wants to do what is right, let him give the people of Canada the benefit of producing the fibre to make binder twine. Why should we pay a million and a half dollars over to the people of the United States, a great portion of it being for labour, instead of keeping it for our own workingmen ? Why should not the farmers of this country, particularly in the North-west, grow the fibre and our Canadian boys manufacture it into binder twine? But we are importing it now to the extent of a million and a half dollars worth from the United States, free of duty, and it comes in here and is sold to our farmers, by the act of this government, and the industries in this country cannot go on without a bonus is paid to them. Now, the minister asks the workingmen of this country, who have no interest in binder twine at all, to help pay that tax. Why should they be compelled to do it ? I say on behalf of the workingmen, that it is unfair to them for the Minister of Finance to put his hand into their pockets and to take out the money to pay this bounty to the manufacturers of binder twine.

I must congratulate the last speaker (Mr. Taylor), who I have now heard for the first time ask why the workingmen should be taxed to provide cheaper articles for other people. I have often been bothered with that question myself, but I have answered it in a different way to what the hon. gentleman usually does. But it appears to me that the greater part of this discussion is not addressed to the main feature of the question. It has been asked, Are we to be under the sufferance of the United States? Well, if the only source of the supply of this fibre is the Philippines, we have got to answer that question in the affirmative, because that country is under the United States. Consequently, we must be under the sufferance of the United States, and it makes no difference whether we get hot about it or not, we are utterly dependent upon another nation. If that is the case, why is this export duty put on ? Is it put on to stimulate protection ? That is the legitimate office of an export duty. It is either that, or it is to stop exportation. But if it is neither of these, then it must be put on for the benefit and at the request of the manufacturers of binder twine in the United States. They have that much leverage on their government that they are able to take that much money out of their people, or out of ours, for their special benefit. Well, if that is the case, it appears to me

tliat if this three-eighths of a cent bounty that we are going to put on offsets the operation of their export duty, then I think it is most probable that they will increase the duty. X want to ask the Minister of Finance a question which he must have been thinking about for some years.
There has been in the southern states a good deal of experiment carried on with the object of proving whether any material can be produced that would take the place of manilla fibre in the manufacture of binder twine. I understand that there has been more or less attention paid to it in this country, but seeing that the matter has been before the Department of Finance for some years, it seems to me that the hon. Minister of Finance must have had his attention drawn to it and that he must have come to some conclusion upon it, and as the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has given his word that we can raise a substitute in the North-west Territories, I certainly agree with him that it would be far better to try and encourage the growing of a substitute in this country than to start upon this policy, knowing that we shall all the while have to keep up with the policy in regard to the exportation of fibre from the Philippine Islands. I may be dense, but it seemed to me, when I read this resolution when it was first put upon the order paper, that that was the whole question. As a matter of fact, Is all the available supply in the Philippine Islands ?
Yes.
That is a fact in respect to manilla.
Is it a fact that there is no substitute that can be provided ?

I speak with some hesitation in regard to a matter of this kind, but I am advised that there has been nothing found which can take the place of manilla for the purpose of cordage or binder twine. There is a substitute, known as sisal, which is raised in the West Indies, and it is used to some considerable extent as a substitute, but it is not as good as the original article. We do not propose to put a bounty on binder twine irrespective of the material used in its manufacture. If it is made from these substitutes imported from abroad, the condition which we are dealing with does not exist and no bounty is paid. We confine the bounty to the quantity of actual manilla used in the manufacture of binder twine. I am not aware that there is any produced in Canada at the present time" and I am not aware that there is any serious proposition at present to raise anything in Canada which would exactly take the place of manilla. We may be able to get something that will be a substitute, but up to the present time, as far as my knowledge goes, there is nothing that
the manufacturers of binder twine would accept as a fair substitute for manilla.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) looks at the Auditor General's Report, he will see the quantity of raw material purchased last year by the government institution at Kingston, and he will find that about one-sixth of the binder twine was the product of manilla, and that the rest was sisal.

Nearly every industry which has had some special source of supply of raw material has had to adapt itself to some other line of material when the original supply had run out. I think it would be as well for the hon. Minister of Finance to pay attention to the matter of finding a fair substitute. At the present time we have to accept the statement, which I believe is the statement of the manufacturers, that there has been nothing so far produced that will take the place of manilla fibre in making binder twine. But if they make binder twine with other material, and if the supply of manilla is limited, we will have to find something else, and it would seem to be the part of wisdom to devote ourselves to an effort to finding a suitable substitute rather than that we should toe trying to protect ourselves when we know we shall not succeed. As to the question whether a bounty is more preferable than a protective duty, I say it is.

I want to answer the question put by the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor). He made, I might almost say, a tearful appeal on'behalf of the workingmen of Canada, who, he said, would be called upon to pay this tax by reason of the bounty. I do not think the workingmen of this country want to be placed in any different position from any other class of the people. The workingmen should pay their proportion of the taxes, just the same as the capitalists do and as the farmers do. I represent, it is true, a very large number of workingmen, and I am satisfied that these workingmen are willing to pay their fair share of taxation. The difference between a duty and a bounty is this : Whereas, under a duty, the party who consumes the article-in this case it is the farmer who is bound to be a consumer of binder twine whether he wishes to be or not-would have to pay that special tax
How is that, when the price is fixed by the American cordage trust ?

I am speaking about the difference between a bounty and a duty. The duty is paid by the person who consumes the article ; whereas, in the case of a bounty, the public at large contribute to it. As I say. the workingmen in my district are satisfied to pay their fair proportion of taxation.
Does the hon. gentleman prefer a bounty to a duty ?

On this particular question that we are discussing now, which is as to whether there shall be a bounty of three-eighths of a cent per pound put upon binder twine in order that our manufacturers of binder twine may be placed on an equality with American manufacturers.

The hon. gentleman has given expression to his approval of the principle of aiding by bounty rather than aiding by a duty. I want to know whether he is in favour of giving aid to an industry by bounty instead of by duty ?
I do not think that is a question I am called upon to answer at the present moment.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) is not bound to answer, of course.

The point we are discussing has nothing to do with that, because we are not discussing whether it is better to put a bounty on or whether it is better to put a duty on. We are discussing the question as to who are the people who have to pay the tax.
The hon. gentleman made the statement that he approved of this proposition to grant a bounty on binder twine, because the community in general did not have to pay it, but the person interested.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: One hon. member on his feet at a time is the rule.

I never know when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is going to get up or sit down. I did not make the statement which he attributes to me. I disagree entirely with wThat he says.
