I did not say that a duty imposed a tax on the community. I said that with a duty a man who is compelled to pay the duty has to pay the tax himself, while in the case of a bounty the public at large-the workingman, the farmer, the capitalist and the manufacturer -all have to pay their proportionate share. That is as far as I went.

The question before the committee is whether the resolution of the hon. Minister of Finance shall pass. We are wandering away from the question and wasting the time of the House, until I am sick and tired listening to this miserable twaddle that is spoken on a question of this kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross) should have got up and made that speech when I decided that hon. members were violating the rules of the House.

I beg to take direct issue with the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Galliher). He has stated that the object of the hon. Minister of Finance in ask-Mr. GALLIHER.
ing us to sanction the principle of giving a bounty is to place the Canadian manufacturer on the same footing as the American manufacturer. Is that it ?
Mr. GALLIHER, With regard to the supply of raw material.

Now, the hon. gentleman is altogether mistaken. He has not given any attention to the question under consideration. He has given no consideration whatever to it. The American manufacturer is protected to-day by a duty of 45 per cent. That is a very high duty indeed, and the Canadian manufacturer has no protection at all. That makes a vast difference. The question is very obvious, it seems to me.
You forget that I was speaking of the home market.

Some of my hon. friends have stated that every time we put a duty on a certain article we are imposing taxes upon the people. That is a false theory. There is not only nothing in it but there is a falsehood in it. There is nothing good in it but there is a great deal of bad in it. When a duty is imposed on an article that we can manufacture here it means that Canadian labour will produce that article instead of foreign labour. For instance in the United States they have a duty of 45 per cent on agricultural implements and agricultural implements sell cheaper in the United States than anywhere else in the world. Is there any reason uuder the sun why Canadian labour cannot manufacture binder twine as cheaply as American labour ?
No.

Why not. We can get our raw material nearly as cheap as they can, and our Canadian labour is cheaper than their's, and I say without hesitation that if the Canadian manufacturer is given the home market he can manufacture just as cheaply and just as advantageously as the American manufacturer can. If we are to be saying all the time that we cannot manufacture as cheaply as the Americans, why then we will never build up industries in this country. Perhaps it is that we have not at present the equipment necessary to supply the demand for binder twine, but let the Minister of Finance say that in two years or in three years the duty will be so and so, let us have a policy and we will soon have the means to manufacture. The giving of bounties is simply taking the money from my pocket and from every other man's pocket without giving to capital any assistance for the future, and the people of this country will never stand paying bounties for all time.
Is it wrong ?
Of course it is wrong.
Is not a duty wrong in the same sense ?

No, and for the excellent reason that if you prevent the products of foreign labour coming into this country and if you give Canadian workmen the advantages that you are giving foreign workmen, you do not increase the price.
What about the consumer V
The consumer is yourself and myself and the consumer will pay the very same price.
That is not what the member for Leeds says ?
Who pays the duty ?
Yes, who pays the duty. Take any article you like that we manufacture in this country and it is folly to say that we are going to pay higher prices for it than we do now.
In many cases.
I say no, and I will prove it. Is there any reason why labourers in Montreal and Toronto, or in Brandon, or in Winnipeg cannot make binder twine as cheaply as the American labourer can.

Possibly not.
Hon. Mi'. TARTE. There is no reason why Canadian money cannot procure the same plant ; there is no reason why Canadian labour should not be as skilful as American labour, and why under the sun could not our Canadian manufacturers sell as cheaply as American manufacturers. I know that I will be told that competition will be less and that this is the only argument, but take the manufacturer of agricultural implements and there are fifty of them in Canada and let us secure the Canadian market for the manufacturer of binder twine, and you will have competition. I do not desire to address myself to free-traders who do not want to be convinced.
There are none here.
There are some of them, and I have no doubt they 'are in perfect good faith.
Very few.
They are getting less.
There will be more after next election.
I heard that speech before.

I am sorry that my hon. friend does not pay more attention to it. In what position have we been during the last two or three years. Why, during the last two years we have been importing 75 per cent of our binder twine from the American trusts, mind you. These Ameri-230
can trusts have gone to the Canadian manufacturer and they have allowed them to manufacture 25 per cent and no more, because they have said to them : You are not protected in Canada and if you manufacture more than the 25 per cent we will slaughter the Canadian market. Is not that a shameful state of things ?
They fixed the price.
Yes, the American trusts were in a position to dictate terms because there was not protection in Canada, and are we going to stand that kind of thing ?
We are getting cheaper binder twine than protection would give us.

Not at all. The freetraders are simply playing the game of the American trusts. I could establish by evidence before a committee of the House to-morrow that the American trusts have dictated their own terms to the Canadian people here. Is it not better that we should have binder twine made by our own people rather than by the American trusts, who are protected by a duty of 45 per cent ? Our farmers themselves have invested money in this industry
Are not the American trusts so far as binder twine is concerned in a position to prevent you manufacturing binder twine in Canada if you had a tariff as high as the roof ?
How could they do that ?
Because they control all the raw material and we are at their mercy for it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You can go to England and buy all you want of it.
England has to pay the export duty.
I do not know that the American trusts control all the raw material, and I would be very much surprised if that were the ease.
There is an immense exportation of it to England that the American trusts cannot touch.

If we were to believe the statements that whenever we impose a duty on foreign articles we are taxing our own people, then there would be no use in our having any industry in this country whatever. But fortunately that theory is utterly false from the very bottom to the very top, and there is no doubt whatever that when a country is in a position to supply our own markets advantageously, as we are capable of doing in many many things, it is our great advantage to do so. Why have we got that' much ? We are

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
creating centres of trade, and giving traffic to our railways and navigation companies and work to our own people. Why are so many of our countrymen in the United States ? Every man who has followed the history of the past knows that it is because we have not enough industries here. Why have our friends in the maritime provinces lost so much of their population ? Because they have not enough industries there. Why are they asking parliament to-day to grant them bounties for their industries ? Because they know that without those favours their industries could not get on their feet. When some of their industries are protected, they say, we are against protection. What is true in the maritime provinces is true everywhere. It is a pity that men of ability and standing feel bound by past theories or ' past speeches. It seems to me they should take the example of such men as Mr. Chamberlain. He has been a partisan of free trade, but he has changed his mind, because he sees that England has been made a slaughter market by all the nations of the world. What is true of England is true of Canada. Our tariff, which is relatively low to-day, is no longer sufficient. Circumstances have changed. It does not do any harm to teach some little lessons to our friends in the maritime provinces. They want railways, they want millions in bounties, and when we ask them to take into consideration the fact that in the other provinces we can manufacture goods for them, they go for us, and in great style. I say that on this occasion the Minister of Finance is making a mistake. During the last five or six years we have tried the system of bounties; we have tried it on lead and on iron, and it has not worked. The Minister of Finance has been obliged to change it three times, and I make this prophesy, that the third change will not work much better than the two first did. If he had come out straight with a reasonable duty on binder twine, he would not be obliged to pay a large sum of money, the Canadian manufacturers would extend their works, the farmers would not have to pay more for their binder twine, and we would have an additional market for our farmers. I am spending the summer at a country place, Boucherville, and the farmers there realize that their best market is the city of Montreal. They sell all their products in that city. Let us create centres of industry in all parts of Canada-binder twine industries, agricultural implement industries, and other industries-in larger proportion. Let us manufacture everything we can.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) We have heard that speech before, often and often.
Then, my hon. friend is assuredly deaf from a fiscal standpoint, otherwise he would have changed his mind after hearing such powerful and convincing arguments.

I would not have said anything but for the hon. gentleman's reference to the maritime provinces. I am not going to discuss the question of protection and free trade with the hon. member; but I wish to point out that he has taken a position today in which he is opposed by all free traders and all protectionists. They all hold that there is no fairer way to assist industries than by bounties, because the general community pay them instead of the few who use the protected article. It will not do for the hon. gentleman to try and set the maritime provinces against the rest of this Dominion. We pay our fair share of a fairly large duty, averaging sixteen or seventeen per cent, on the goods we buy. We are manufacturers of iron, and if we get a bounty to help us a little in starting our industries, surely the hon. gentleman is not going to hold us up as wanting everything and giving nothing. I make the statement that any industry that cannot flourish on a protection of seventeen or eighteen per cent must have something wrong with it. With regard to binder twine, the cry of everybody in this House was : take the duty off binder twine in the interest of the farmer. We took off the duty and the farmers started a binder twine industry of their own; and, if I am correctly informed, that industry paid one hundred per cent on the capital invested, so that in one year they got their whole capital back. An industry that can do that ought to be able to stand a little competition from the United States. I do not know altogether the conditions in regard to the raw material for binder twine.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentlemen who say ' hear, hear,' are idiotic enough to think they do. I am honest enough to say I do not know all the conditions affecting the raw material; but I do know that when there is a difference in the cost of the raw material that enters into the manufacture of the article in the United States and in Canada, and the United States manufacturer has that advantage because of a law of the United States, it is only fair to the Canadian manufacturer that he should be put in the same position.
What about the forty-five per cent duty ?

If the American manufacturers have a forty-five per cent duty, and they can sell the article in Canada cheaper than the men who made a hundred per cent on the money they invested in one year, I say let it come in the interest of the farmers. I am on the side of the farmer who purchases rather than the few manufacturers who manufacture. To hear hon. gentlemen opposite one would suppose that the manufacturer was everything. He is a good deal, I admit, but he only represents about twelve per cent of the population of Canada, and I think a few of us

should say something in the interest of the eighty-eight per cent of people who purchase. Hon. gentlemen opposite think that if we manufactured everything here and kept out foreign goods, that would be a good thing.
Hear, hear.
Where, then, would you get money to pay the cost of the railways 1
Where do the United States get their revenue ?

The United States get it on the goods they import; but the man who uses the article which is made in the country pays a large duty on it, not to the government, but to the manufacturer who puts up the price as near as he can to the price of the article imported plus the duty. I am in favour of looking after all classes; but it makes a man tired) to be told constantly that there is only one class in the country to be looked after, namely, the manufacturers. How are you going to enrich the farmers who constitute sixty-five or seventy per cent of the people of Canada, by enabling them to feed the fifteen per cent who are engaged in manufacturing 1
Mr, CLANCY. Where does the hon. gentleman get his calculation ?
If the hon. gentleman looks at the census, he will find that my statement is correct.
I say it is not correct.

My statement is correct. The large influx of population into this country at the present time is composed of farmers, and the millions of acres of land in the North-west are going to be occupied by men engaged in tilling the soil; so that instead of diminishing the number of farmers in Canada, we are increasing it. I think that the manufacturers are entitled to consideration, and when we give them an advantage of sixteen per cent, we give them a good start. The farmer who has to sell his products in the markets of the world has no such advantage; he has no bounty or duty or anything else to help him; and after being obliged to meet the competition of every other man in the markets of the world, he is to be taxed, not by the government or for the public requirements, but by the protectionists tax collector in order to build up his industry. I want the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) to understand that the sentiment in the maritime provinces on this subject is just about the same as I find it to be in every other part of Canada, namely, that when the duties we have gave a reasonable chance to manufacture, we should not increase them.
What about the duty on binder twine ?

I would not have a duty on binder twine. And the hon. gentleman 230J
(Mr. Sproule) or, if not he, a large number of hon. gentlemen of the same persuasion, kept this House hour after hour and day after day while they sought to make capital out of a proposal to take the duty off binder twine. It seemed to be a race between some hon. gentlemen on that side and some hon. gentlemen on this side as to who should speak most kindly of this proposal in the effort to relieve the farmers of their sufferings caused by the duty that then existed.
The hon, gentleman (Mr. Fraser) does not mean to say that I advocated the removal of the duty on binder twine ?
I venture to say the hon. gentleman did not say a word in favour of keeping it on when hon. gentlemen on his own side advocated its removal.
Time and time again I did. I never yet advocated taking the duty off. But I have often advocated keeping it on.

The difficulty I am in is that the hon. gentleman speaks so often that it would be a weary hunt for me to go through ' Hansard ' to find out what he said on any particular question. I accept the hon. gentleman's statement that he was in favour of the duty, and that whenever an hon gentleman on his own side declared in favour of taking it off, he rose and contended ardently to have it left on.
That is entirely a misrepresentation of what I said.

Then, the hon. gentleman did not oppose those on his own side who advocated the removal of the duty ? That is what I said-that when his own side advocated taking it off, he did not advocate keeping it on-and the hon. gentleman agrees with me.
The hon. gentleman is not at all correct.

I considered then as I do now that it was a little race between hon. gentlemen opposite and hon. gentlemen on this side for popularity with the farmers. All agreed in saying that if the duty were taken off the farmers would get their binder twine for less.
Surely, the hon. gentleman (Air. Fraser) is not now insisting that there ever was a movement on this side, or ever a speech made on this side, in favour of taking the duty off.
Alost decidedly. The late Air. Davin, then member for West Assin-iboia, was the chosen champion, the very apostle of the removal of this duty.

Obstruction.

There is not a political economist of standing, whether he takes the free trade or the protectionist side, but admits that, if anything is to be done in favour of a particular manufacture, the right way is to do it by means of a bounty. If I alluded to the maritime provinces, it is only because I was interrupted by some of my friends from that part of the country. In answer to them, I gave what I thought a pretty good argument. I simply told them that when the iron industries were involved they

were very glad to have recourse to what they call now the best form of protection. Nobody agreed more cheerfully to help the iron industry than I did. But I believe we did not do in 1897 what we are called upon to do now. When we were arranging duties on iron and steel in the revision of 1897, the country was not equipped as it is now. And I claim that, instead of giving bounties to-day, the country, being better equipped, having more iron and steel plants, the time has come for the imposition of duties. I believe that is the genuine position to take.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) a question ? Does this argument of his apply to the maritime provinces only ?
Certainly not.

I stated the reason. I was interrupted by two or three of my friends from the maritime provinces, and I answered them. Now I expect my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) to take part in this debate. I am going to call him to my help and rescue. I need some help just now. I will tell him why I invite him to take part in this debate. He knows better than I do the facts concerning the binder twine industry in Brantford, his own town. I was a minister of the Crown with the hon. gentleman when the farmers' binder twine mills made money. I was a minister of the Crown with him when the same men came to us and told us that they could not go on with their operations. And they have closed their mill. Many of the binder twine mills have been closed or are working only partially. The Minister of Customs knows the case better than I do, but I know something about it, and I will tell what I know for the information of my hon. friends. The American factories, being unable to get supplies, our people made money
Out of the raw material ?

a duty of 45 per cent. I have the statement in my hand about those big industries.
They put no money in it.

They got it all back.

Because the American trust have come to this country and have given the Canadian manufacturers to understand that if they dare to manufacture more than 25 per cent they would slaughter them. I make this statement on my responsibility, and if the government institute an inquiry they will find that to be the ease. Why should we allow that ? Why is that state of affairs going on ? Because there is no protection against the foi'eign manufacturer. Now is it desirable that we should go on in that way ? Sir, no childish arguments can be advanced against that clear fact. We have imported 75 per cent of an article that we can produce ourselves, for which we have the plant, but our plant has been kept idle by the American trust. I am speaking in the presence or the right hon. gentleman who leads the government, and I make the statement again, it is true and can be proved in twenty-four hours. Now, is it desirable that we should continue in that way. Are convinced free traders going to get up in this parliament and say that it is a satisfactory condition of affairs that an American trust should be given permission to come into this country and say to our Canadian manufacturers :	You are
not protected ; we are protected by a 45 per cent duty ; you cannot compete against us, and we can slaughter you because we have no protection. Both parties in this country are responsible for that state of affairs. The late Minister of Finance, influenced by the same considerations that we hear to-day, lowered the duty to 124 per cent. He made a mistake, and we have made another mistake by wiping out the duty. We had to lose something in order to save more. I felt obliged to consent to this, because I thought it was necessary to make some sacrifice in order to save something more important. But now by-gones are by-gones. The Minister of Finance and his colleagues understand so well that the binder twine industry cannot go on under the present conditions, that they are asking us to
give a bounty. Now, I say that bounties are not the best way to deal with this matter. I say that instead of asking us to take the money out of the pockets of the Canadian tax-payers, we should prevent the American trust from invading our market. There is no sense in the argument, there is no truth in the assertion. But what is true of binder twine is true of everything else. Let me explain this matter. When a point is raised in the committee upon which the committee wish to obtain the decision of the Speaker, a motion may be made for the committee to rise and report progress, and place the point in dispute before the Speaker, who will then, in his place, submit the matter to the House for its consideration, and afterwards give his decision upon the point raised. When there is an appeal made from the decision of the chairman, the mode of procedure is somewhat different. The Speaker simply takes the Chair and the chairman steps out without any motion at all. Then the Speaker puts the question to the House, shall the decision of the Chairman be sustained ? And if the decision is sustained, the Speaker steps out and the chairman steps into his place. Now, let me quote the rule from Bourinot. The rule is first given, and then the methods which

were employed iu 1885, when there were several appeals to the Speaker j
In such a case it is for the chairman of the committee to report in writing the point of order wihieh he has decided, and the Speaker must then submit the matter to the House in the language reported to him, and put the question, that the decision of the chairman he confirmed. The committee may then resume if the business be not concluded.
