speechtext: The House resumed in committee the resolution concerning a bounty on binder twine.

At six o'clock when the committee rose, I was saying that all the enlightened nations in the world were engaged in the battle of industrial life. I mentioned some nations, and included the name Russia. There was a clamour of scornful disdain at the mention of that country. I have no objection to withdraw the name of Russia in discussing a question of this kind. I think it is useless, it is unfair, to look at straws, let us look at square facts. A little flaw in a big piece of steel does not make much difference. However. Russia is not such a small nation that we must ignore it. Russia is euteriug into the field of industrial activity with a surprising strength. It is one of the great coming nations of the world industrially, and agriculturally it is to-day; one of the great nations of the world. Canada has no more dangerous rival for wheat than Siberia. However, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is asking us to-day to deal with a special case, with the binder twine industry. He is giving to that industry a stone when he has been asked to give bread. He was not asked to give bounties. My hon. friend from British Columbia (Mr. Macpherson), who I do not see in the House at this moment. defended bounties. When his friends in British Columbia approached parliament about lead, they did not ask for a bounty, they asked for protective duties. Let me say that the iron and steel capitalists of Sydney have not asked for a bounty either, they ask for a straight protective duty. But they must submit to the inevitable, and they have informed the government that the inevitable to which they submit will not lead them to final success. That is the reason why, in my humble opinion, the government is not following the course that they should follow. They recognize the fact that the industries to' which they are giving bounties cannot live without something more.
The hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has made the statement that the lead people who came here did not ask for a bounty.
No, they asked for duties.
I wish to tell the hon. gentleman that they did ask for one of the two things. It was immaterial to them which, and quite a number of them favoured the bounty.

Let my hon. friend (Mr. Macpherson) give me that assurance and I will give him the paper which I have in my hands, the memorandum presented to myself and my former colleagues by these very same men. I have the memorandum and I will pledge myself to bring it and lay it on the Table of the House.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman to the contrary notwithstanding, I attended the first meeting that was held by the silver lead men of British Columbia, in the city of Vancouver, when they talked it over, and talked it over very strongly, and I can assure the hon. gentleman and the committee that the question of bounties was talked of as much as the question of duties-every bit as much. I cannot help what he may have in his hands. I know that the silver lead men were very well pleased to get a bounty, that they were glad to get it and that that was part of their suggestion.

The hon. gentleman is in a very peculiar position indeed. Two years ago a bounty was given. The system of bounty which was then adopted did not produce anything. He knows that. His friends in the west could not take advantage of it. The lead industry could not take advantage of the system of bounty that was then adopted. How then can he say that it was a good system ?
It was not high enough.

It was not sufficient then. The system of bounty then adopted, for which, I admit, I was responsible, did not work. Of course, the lead people are obliged to accept what they are given, because the government stated at the beginning of the session through the hon. Minister of Finance that they would not give any duties. They are bound to accept what they are given. But the lead people, not only to-day, but for years, have been asking for duties. The iron people have been asking for duties, the people interested in the binder twine industry have been asking also for duties and not for bounties. These are the facts of the case. So, I say that we are face to face with the fact that the government have fully made up their mind that they will not adopt the policy of protecting the national industries of the country. It is debatable. I frankly admit that there are two sides to this question. I do not claim to be infallible. Those who hold the view that a low system of tariff is the best, have the full right to their views, but let the country know where we stand. The government should tell us where they stand to-day. Am I mistaken in saying'that in the not very far past, even during this session, members of the government have been giving hints-very strong hints-pledges, I may say, to the manu-

facturers, that in the near future the tariff will be revised on the protectionist system and that these hints have been given by ministers of the Crown, by responsible men? Yet, to-day we hear prominent supporters of the government denouncing protection in all sorts of forms. Well what I ask, for one, is that we may know exactly where we stand. The system of bounties is protection in a certain form. There is no doubt whatever that industries that are given bounties will benefit by them. If you give to a certain manufacturer $5 a ton or five cents a pound, that is so much that the manufacturer will put in his pocket. There is no doubt about that. But that is not the policy of protection that I for one believe this country should adopt. I have no more to say except that in my opinion the government are making a mistake in this case, not only from the industrial standpoint, not only from the financial standpoint, but from the standpoint of the farmers. A large quantity of Canadian flax is used in the manufacture of twine and small cordage. The Canadian farmers, if we had a protective policy, would be protected then. The' more people we employ in this country the more goods we manufacture here, the bigger we make the market for the Canadian farmer. We imported during the last two or three years 75 per cent of the twine and cordage that we are using. If we had manufactured that twine and cordage we would have employed some Canadian labour, we would have bought some Canadian wheat, we would have kept in the country hundreds of thousands of dollars that we sent abroad. These facts cannot be disputed. Every half million dollars or million dollars of money that are kept in circulation in this country to buy Canadian goods, to buy flour, to buy timber, to buy iron, to buy meat is money that is better employed than if it is sent abroad to feed foreign labourers, to buy foreign timber and to buy foreign products of other kinds. It seems to me that the argument is unanswerable. I fully grant that no country in the world can produce everything that it needs, but if a country can manufacture an article advantageously, I do not see any reason why it should be manufactured outside of its limits. Now, I have been interrupted several times by the words 'look at England.' I have already, on a former occasion, answered that argument, but I believe the best answer for that argument is being given day after day through the despatches that are coming from the mother land. Let us not forget that England has not always been a free trade country-very far from it.
Since 1842.
My hon. friend from 'Victoria (Mr. Ross) says that England has been a free trade country since 1842. He is mistaken.	'	I
I am always mistaken.

No, the hon. gentleman is not always mistaken, but this time he is mistaken as to that, and if he will kindly follow me for one minute I will prove that he is mistaken in his statement. No doubt the first step towards the principle of free trade was taken in 1842, but the last duties were removed only in 1860, when there remained only 24 articles on the dutiable list. What happened then ? There was a war between Austria and Germany, there was a war between France and Prussia, and there was the great civil war in the United States. In other words, the nations of the world which have come to the front since as industrial nations were not equipped practically then, and these nations have been equipped only since 1875, after the Franco-Prussian war. Well now, England had been for many years before a violently protective country. England has been losing ground rapidly. The balance of trade has been year after year against England. I gave the figures the other day, and nobody has answered them, and they cannot be answered, because they are true. The agriculture of England has been destroyed year after year ; the acreage under cultivation has diminished to a lamentable extent. These facts cannot be disputed. Now the foremost men of England, the far sighted men of England realize that England is losing ground all over the world, and there is a strong movement towards the adoption of a protective tariff, because they feel the time has come, the conditions being changed in regard to the nations of the world, when England must not be any longer the dumping ground of the universe. At the same time Canada is face to face with a unique occasion. The policy of Mr. Chamberlain has the right ring about it-the right imperial ring and the right colonial ring. We can get a preference from England provided we make up our minds that we are going to be a protectionist country. If we open our markets to all nations of the earth and say they shall have equal rights, then we cannot get a preference from England. We must raise our tariff against the nations of the world if we are to trade with the motherland. This is not a question of theory. For the last fifty years our tariff has been about half the tariff of our American friends. The United States has developed year after year, until now they have a population of 80,000,000. We have a little less than 6,000,000 ; we have not progressed so fast ; their tariff is twice as high as ours. The lesson that the United States has taught us should not be lost sight of. We cannot help ourselves. Those of us who hold views contrary to the views of the present government are in the minority, apparently at any rate. I doubt very much if we are in the minority in this country ; I believe we are

in the majority at this very moment. In the Liberal party itself we are not in the minority, but I know what party ties are and I know what party discipline is. There are members of parliament sitting on this side of the House who share the views I have expressed. There are on the ministerial benches ministers of the Crown who share my views. It is an old story for me ; I know all about it. There are in all the provinces Liberals of strong views-I have their letters in my hand-there are strong Liberals who do not hesitate to write me day by day that the government is wrong. I do not say that they will vote against the government, because they still have hopes. That is the trouble, if I may call it a trouble. I say now, in all candour, that I would rather stand by the word ' hope.' The ministers are giving the hope to their friends who are protectionists that they will revise the tariff, but there are still some of their supporters who say that a low tariff is a good tariff. That is not a right stand, in my humble opinion. It may not be the last time that we shall call the attention of the country to the opinions we hold. The fiscal policy of a country should be above petty party division, and should be considered a question apart from politics. In conclusion, Sir, I wish to say that I accept the bounty, because I cannot get duties.

This subject has been pretty well threshed out this afternoon, and I rise simply because of some references that have been made by the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte). In two particulars the hon. gentleman has done a valuable public service. In the first place, he took his stand upon what I consider to be sound economic doctrine ; and in the second place, he succeeded in showing the falsity of one of the cries which our hon. friends of the opposition-notwithstanding that they were his chief applaud-ers here this afternoon-have for many months been holding forth to the people of Canada. I refer to the contention of hon. gentlemen opposite that it was the action of the government in 1897, in removing the duty from binder twine, which caused the considerable increase in its price. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has pointed to us the binder twine factory in Brantford, which in two years yielded a dividend to the proprietors exceeding 100 per cent, and he told us that the reason why they could make such enormous profit was on account of the Spanish-American war, which caused the increase in the value of the raw material, a stock of which these gentlemen, to their own great profit, happened to have on hand. It would appear then that in the opinion of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) the Spanish-American war had something to do with the increase in the price of binder twine, and that it was not the action of the government in removing the duty which was the cause of that increase. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) also stated that he was opposed to this bounty, because it meant taking the money out of the pockets of some people in the country and putting it into the pockets of other people. And when I asked if the same principle should not be applied to duties, he said it should ; but he contended that the duty did not increase the price. His statement meant that if it could be shown to him that a duty upon an article increased the price he would oppose that duty, because it would be improperly taking money out of the pockets of some people of the country and putting it by law into the pockets of other people. He argued, however, that the placing of a duty on binder twine would not increase its price. I believe, Sir, in considering any one of these articles upon its merits in connection with the imposition of a duty, and it may very well be that the placing of a duty on some articles would not lead to an increase in their price. However, as regards twine, I think the opposite, and a very large number of the farmers of this country think the opposite. But I say that it may be possible, notwithstanding my own opinion and the opinion of others, that the placing of a duty on binder twine would not increase the price of the article, and therefore, so far as binder twine is concerned, if the hon. gentleman be correct in his theory, his position is perfectly sound. But in taking the position that the placing of a duty on articles in general does not enhance the price, my hon. friend is flying in the teeth of every economic authority in this country or in any other country. I could point him to the utterance of the Hon. George E. Foster, who said on one occasion that if the putting of the duty on an article did not have the effect of enhancing its price, then it would be entirely useless to impose a duty. My hon. friend must be aware that when he declares that the putting of a duty on articles of general commerce does not enhance their price, he is announcing an opinion which is the very opposite of the opinion held by a very large number of people in Canada. Why do the consumers object to any proposition to increase the tariff ? They may be mistaken, and their opinion may not be worth as much as the opinion of the hon. member for St. Mary's, but they certainly do think that an increase in the duty would mean an increase in the price. And when the hon. gentleman speaks of the large body of opinion in this country in favour of the doctrine which he has been promulgating for some months, he must forget that we had farmers' associations throughout the province of Ontario meeting week after week, and at every meeting placing themselves on record as being opposed to any general increase in the tariff. He must also forget that the Trades and Labour Council of Canada, at its last annual meeting, placed on record a most emphatic protest against any general increase in the tariff.
Would the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him if he believes that the Trades and Labour Council represent the labour element of this country on that point ?
I should hope so.
My hon. friend hopes in vain.

My opinion upon that point may not be worth a great deal, but, at all events, this body represents a section of labouring people from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and their view is entitled to some respect.
Certainly it is.

And when my hon. friend was contending that no duty meant an increase in price, I remembered a statement which X saw in a reputable newspaper some weeks ago with regard to the prices of wire. It will be remembered that when changes were made in the tariff some years ago, barb wire for fencing and certain other qualities of wire, technically designated by numbers, were placed upon the free list. There are certain other qualities of wire which still bear a duty. I saw the statement made in the ' Farmers' Sun ' of Toronto, and I have never seen it denied, that the difference in the price of the wire which is free of duty in Canada, as compared with the United States, is 25 cents per 100 pounds, and on these qualities of wire which still bear a duty in Canada, there is a difference in price of $1.60 per 100 pounds as against 25 cents per 100 pounds on the wire that is free of duty.
What is the difference on that class of wire to which the hon. gentleman refers ?
Barbed wire and certain other brands are free, and certain other qualities remain dutiable.
What is the duty on that ?
I imagine it is twenty or twenty-five per cent.
Would that make $1.60 per cwt V
I presume so. I was led to believe so by the statements of the * Farmers' Sun.'
Would the hon. gentleman tell me what it is worth per hundred.

I am not an expert in wire. I am simply presenting the statement as I have obtained it. I have never heard a denial of the statement. If any hon. gentleman is prepared to deny it, the House will no doubt be very glad to have the information. The statement was that on one class of wire which is free there is only a differ-erenee of 25 cents per cwt., which is only Mr. SCOTT.
the difference of the transportation charges, while the wire which is dutiable shows a difference in price between the United States and Canada of $1.60 per cwt., which is the difference in the cost of transportation and the duty added, showing conclusively that the farmers have to pay a higher price for those articles on which duties are levied. If the placing of a duty on an article does not mean any increase in price, what is the meaning of the appeal which hon. gentlemen opposite are from time to time making in this House for increased duties for the benefit of the farmers ? How are the farmers going to be benefited if the increased duties are not going to increase the prices of the products they raise ? As I said before, there may be certain articles on which the placing of a duty would not increase the price ; but there are other articles on which the duty increases the price almost to the level of the duty. For what other purpose is it proposed to place a duty on steel rails ? Will any hon. gentleman say that that is not intended to give the manufacturers an enhanced price on that article ?

The hon. gentleman knows that steel rails are free. He knows that if a duty of $7 a ton were put on steel rails, we would have the Canadian market for steel rails, and it does not necessarily follow that there would be any advance in price.

When Mr. Clergue last fall ajjpealed for a duty on steel rails, what was the reason underlying his appeal ? It was that Mackenzie & Mann were buying steel rails in Germany at a price which he could not hope to compete with, and he wanted a duty so as to compel Mackenzie & Mann and other railway builders in this country to pay a higher price. He said that if that were not done, he could not manufacture steel rails in this country. With regard to the resolution before the House, while I am not at all enthfisiastic in its support or in support of any proposition increasing the taxation of the people of this country, whether by this method or by the method of a customs duty, still, speaking for myself, I very much prefer this method of assisting the binder twine industry to the method of placing a duty on the article. I think this is the much more definite and satisfactory method. If it is in the general interest of the country that any manufacturer should be given direct assistance. I think that the whole country, which it is presumed will receive the benefit, should assist in bearing the burden, instead of the whole burden being placed upon a limited number of consumers who use the article.
Will the hon. gentleman tell the House what benefit the country will derive from this bounty of three-eighths of a cent a pound on manilla fibre ?

I would prefer that my hon. friend should ask the binder twine manufac-

turers that question. I have no distinct knowledge on the matter. But, I presume that the binder twine manufacturers are willing to accept this measure, otherwise I do not suppose that the hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches would be forcing such a measure upon them.

They will be able to sell their binder twine that much cheaper to the consumers.
Hon. Mr. TARTE, In other words, they will be able to compete with the Americans who have closed them up, until to-day seventy-five per cent of the binder twine used in the country is imported. That bounty, I hope, will enable our manufacturers to compete and to keep their establishments open ; so that, instead of importing seventy-five per cent of our binder twine from the United States, we will manufacture it ourselves.
Has the hon. member for St. Mary's any evidence that the binder twine factories have been closed on account of the competition *f the United States ?
Yes.
Is there not evidence to show that the binder twine factories have had all the work they could do for the last three years V
No.
What have they to come here for, then ?

Like other manufacturers, I suppose, to get all they can out of the people of Canada. I suppose the hon. gentleman would say that the manufacturers of threshing machines and binders should come here for more protection, though we know as a matter of fact, that all the manufacturers of binders in Canada were not able to supply the demand of file west last year. If it had not been for the binders that were imported from the United States, half the crop of last year would have remained on the ground unthreshed.
Is the hon. gentleman opposed to this bounty ?

I am asking for information. I think that this government, before they increase the duties or the bounties should be in possession of undoubted facts, and not simply take the statements of the manufacturers themselves. I believe that all these binder twine factories, except two are in the hands of the combine in the United States. I believe that that combine owns these factories, and it is merely to increase their profits that this combine is asking for this bounty.
If this bounty passes, does the hon. gentleman think it will increase the price of binder twine to the farmers ?

speakerposition: topic

speechtext: I do not think it will.
Then, in his opinion, protection does not increase the price to the consumer V

That is a different thing. I believe, from what I could learn from the binder twine manufacturers of the United States, that, as a matter of fact, they never got the rebate to which they were entitled, on account of the peculiar agreement made with the Philippine Islands. So that I do not think the Canadian binder twine manufacturers to-day are suffering at all. I think they are merely trying to get more profit from the sale of their goods.

Has the hon. gentleman any positive information as to the statement he has just made, that nearly all the manufacturers of binder twiiie in Canada are in the hands of the American trusts? If my hon. friend is right, the bounty policy is a very bad one indeed, because we are simply taking money from the pockets of the Canadian people and giving it to the American trusts. That would be an abominable policy, against which the country should revolt. But I believe my hon. friend is wrong. I have positive information that most of the hinder twine industries in Canada are in the hands of Canadians. I have personal information as to that. So that the most of our money will not go to the American trusts. But it shows, if my hon. friend will allow me to say so with all respect and deference, to what extremes our free trade friends will go.

I merely asked the hon. member for St. Mary's for information. He makes a statement of fact on which he has no more reliable information than I have for the statement I made. He has only the rumours circulated through the press and otherwise, and that is the only basis I have for my statement.	.
I would ask the hon. member for St. Mary's how many of these factories are shut down at the present time ?
There are a couple closed down at Brantford.
They are not closed.

My hon. friend will not play on words. They are not closed, but they have not been working on full time nor making money. In Montreal our manufacturers of binder twine have been closed for most of the time.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: How many ?

We have two. One of them is a very large industry. In Brantford there is a large factory established by farmers. I believe a couple of thousand farmers have invested money in it. They have come to us repeatedly and told us they

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: are losing money. And I have received letters from them since. They have had their factory going for only a part of the time. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance knows that as well as I do.
The Chatham factory is closed.

Yes, and most of the factories have been working very little. Let me repeat the statement I made, evidence of which can be had in twenty-four hours if an investigation is held. We imported last year 75 per cent of the binder twine we used. And the American manufacturers came here with threats in their mouths telling our people they must agree to manufacture so much and do no more, or they would slaughter the market. I make this statement deliberately, and am prepared to give the evidence to support it.
I never heard it.
If my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) will induce his friends on the treasury benches to grant an investigation, I will produce the proof of it under oath. It is a fact well known in commercial circles.
I would ask whether any of these factories which are shut down receive pay for shutting down ? The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is in with these people, and I would be glad if he would tell us.

I am not interested in any of these binder twine factories. But I know that the statements I have made are true. The Canadian manufacturers came to us when I was a member of the government asking for protection for their industry. There is no secret about it. They told us they could not compete against the Americans, because the Americans were protected by a duty of 45 per cent, and they were slaughtering this market. The best evidence of all this is that the Finance Minister and the government are asking parliament to vote bounties to these people. Will my hon. friend (Mr. McEwen) vote against these bounties 1 Does he believe that the decision of the government is wrong ? If he thinks this industry is all right, he should vote against this bounty. If these lion, gentlemen are advocating the necessity of additional bounties, how can they say that there is nothing the matter with this industry ? Their position is most illogical. The proposition that the government has laid before us proves that the statements I am making are true and that this industry needs help. I contend that, instead of giving bounties we should put on duties. But I say again that I am very glad that my friends on the treasury benches are not allowing more industries to be closed, but are going to help the Canadian labour to do better than it has done during the past two or three years.

I am sure the government deserves the sympathy in the pitiable position in which they find themselves in regard to this industry. Previous to 1894, there was a sufficient duty on binder twine to enable the manufacturers in Canada to secure nearly all our home market. In 1894, the duty was reduced in deference to clamour raised by people in different parts' of the country for political purposes. With a duty reduced to 124 per cent, the amount of binder twine imported from the United States increased and the amount manufactured in this country decreased. In 1897, the duty was taken off. This was not done because the farmers asked for it. The farmers were not paupers ; they do not ask to be placed in a different posit ion from other people in this country. They know that our revenue is raised by tariff duties, and no person could contend that 121 per cent was an oppressive duty. It is not more than a revenue duty, even according to the views of the members of the government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) has said again and again that the present revenue is a tariff for revenue only, and it is a great deal higher than 124 per cent. So, this duty was not removed because it was a protective duty ; its removal was simply designed as a vote-catcher. The leader of the Liberal party thought the farmers of this country were easily caught, and to catch them they made a few clap-trap changes in the tariff.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) permit me to ask him a question? If the removal of the duty in 1897 was intended as a vote-catcher, what was the object in 1894, in reducing it from 25 per cent to 124 per cent ?

No doubt, it was removed in deference to a political agitation carried on by men who wished to catch votes. All the hou. gentlemen opposite were engaged in it, as well as some on this side. Under the 124 per cent duty we imported only 2.000,000 pounds of binder twine. But when the duty was taken off. the amount increased to 10,000,000 pounds the year before last, and to 15,000,000 pounds last year. Instead of manufacturing 75 per cent of the binder twine we use, we only manufacture 25 per cent, the remainder being imported from the United States where tile manufacture of it gives employment to American workmen. And the farmers are not benefited by it. Even if they were- which I dispute-it would be a benefit which they have never asked for. for they know that every man should contribute his share to the revenue, and 124 per cent is not excessive. Our factories are closed, and the American trust controls our market. If the American trust saw fit. thev could crush our factories out at once. Why ? Because they carry on business in a much larger way and are able to manufacture cheaper

than can the factories in this country. Today, they are placed in a very much superior position because of the f cent per pound that they get. So, the government come to the rescue of this industry. Why do they not do the same by scores of other industries that are in the same position ? Why, because there is not enough money in the treasury to pay bounties on all these industries ? If this system was adopted in its entirety the government would not have one-tenth of the money they would require. Consequently it is adopted piecemeal-a sop thrown here or there wherever there is a strong kick coming. If my hon. friend from Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) comes with a big boot and threatens a strong kick, there is some help given to an industry in his constituency. And an industry in Sydney is treated in me same way and for similar reasons. But the general industries of the country are sacrificed-not all of them, lie-cause the duties were not removed from all of them, were not even lowered on all of them. If to-day we are prosperous these industries are able to survive. But we know what the position of this country was from 1873 to 1879. We had a low tariff, and the hard times in the United States forced the manufacturers there to look for an outside market. They found it in Canada, slaughtering the industries of this country right and left. In 1879 a tariff was put on which enabled our own industries to exist. But the same conditions will arise again unless the government is prepared to keep our market for our own manufacturers.
I think we should adopt a strong tariff in this country for other reasons The Hon. Joseph Chamberlain to-day, in the old country. is holding out his hands to us and making us an offer that will be worth countless millions to this country if we can take advantage of it. But we are not in a position to take advantage of it, we have not anything to offer. Let us raise our tariff, not. as some lion, gentlemen opposite have said, we desire to do, up to that of the United States. No one on this side of the House ever expressed a wish for a tariff the same as they have in the United States. What we want is a tariff averaging that of the United States, a much higher tariff than we have at the present time. Let us place ourselves in that strong position that we will have something to offer, and what will be the consequence ? If we are able to effect with England a preferential arrangement that will enable our products to be placed in her markets at an advantage over those of all other countries, the consequence to this country will be that every acre of land that is capable of producing wheat will be worth at least 820 an acre more. If the farmer only gets five cents a bushel more for his wheat, that will mean $1 on twenty bushels which would be the interest on 820, and the result will be that every acre of land in this country that pro-2314
duces wheat will be advanced in value by 820. But England will not give us this advantage, we cannot expect England to admit our products into her markets on more favourable terms than those of other countries, unless we have something to give in exchange, and we are not in a position today to give anything in exchange. In order that we may have something to give, let us raise our tariff and put ourselves in such a position that we can say to England: we will take down this wall, we will admit your products on extremely favourable terms if you will give us this advantage. Why. Sir, it would be the greatest boon that ever befel this country, and it seems to me this government ought to take some steps in that direction. Now is the time for this government to act, when this agitation is going on in England, when people there are making up their minds. Now is the time when we should advance every argument possible to strengthen the hands of our friends in the old country who are willing to give us preferential treatment,
| treatment that will make this country advance in prosperity far more rapidly than I it is doing now, beyond even the brightest I dreams of our most enthusiastic statesmen. If we could get this preferential treatment people would come to this country from other lands in far greater numbers than they do now. They are to-day coming into the United States at the rate of from 500,000 to SOO.OOO a year. We want to draw the tide of immigration to our own country.
Not all of them.

Not some of them, I agree, because 00 per cent of those people we do not want. But there is a large stream of desirable immigrants coming to America that would form a very desirable addition to our population. The way to induce a greater stream of immigration is to make it more profitable for the farmer to grow agricultural products in this country, and it will be more profitable for him if we can get this advantage in the British market. But we must have something to offer in return-not a mere sop in the way of bounties, such as the government are throwing out to the binder twine industry, which is indeed a very picayune advantage. It is only enabling these manufacturers to hold their heads above water. It does not enable that industry to thrive as it ought. With even the small duty that existed before. instead of our binder twine factories existing by sufferance of the American trust, they would to-day be manufacturing all the twine used in this country. Why should we not make twine in this country sufficient to supply our own wants ? Why do we not make it ? Simply because the binder twine industry is chiefly in the hands of an American trust. It has been alleged here to-day that they made 100 per cent profit. That is true ns concerns the Brant-

ford factory, but how did they do it ? They did it by accumulating the raw material when it was cheap, and selling it when it was dear. That was one reason, but the chief reason was that they took advantage of the enormous rise in price that was caused by the American trust getting control of our markets. They put the price up, and the Brantford company were not foolish enough to throwT away the opportunity, and they sold their twine at the higher price.
I think that company has never paid less than 10 per cent.
If they are paying 10 per cent to-day, I do not know what they are coming to the government for.
Are you opposed to it ?

I believe they should have a higher protection, that would be more valuable to them, and to every other twine industry that saw lit to start business in this country. Gentlemen who argue against the protective tariff lose sight of the fact that it secures a home market to the manufacturers. One of the greatest advantages any industry can have is a market, that is the main thing. Let any company get possession of a market, and it requires a desperate fight on the part of any other company to get that marker away from them. Let them treat their customers fairly, and no new company will be able to undersell them. In 1896 the Canadian manufacturers had possession of a considerable portion of our market, but the American manufacturers have got possession of it, and they will retain possession until our manufacturers are placed in a superior position which will enable them to undersell their American competitors. I am glad indeed that the government has seen fit to offer this little assistance, small as it is. I am glad to know that the light has broken in upon them to this small extent, and I hope they will go further and give these industries, a protective tariff.

I am pleased to know that the government has, even at this late hour, taken some means to help the binder twine factories of Canada out of the hole they have got into for the want of some protection. We are told by the Finance Minister that nearly a year a go the Americans imposed a duty on the raw material. I think it was then the duty of this government, in view of that fact, at the earliest date, at least on the 13tli of March, to introduce this bounty resolution, and to give the binder twine factories a chance to live. But the government have waited until the 24th of July when the market is crowded with American twine. You cannot drive through any town in this country without seeing the shops filled with American binder twine, and that, too, at a time when the Mr. SMITH (Wentworth).
harvest is almost ready to cut. Not until now lias this government given the binder twine people any idea that they were going to be assisted.
The hou. gentleman has forgotten the statement made in the Budget Speech that this bounty would be paid.
The hon. gentleman did not indicate what the nature of the assistance would be.
The binder twine men understood it.

I am glad the government has now come to the relief of the binder twine men, and is going to give them something for what they manufactured last year, because they had no assurance at all that they would even get this bounty. We have heard many things pr mised in the speech from the Throne that were never performed. .

This is the language used by the Finance Minister :
The government will introduce, before the close of the session, some legislation whereby the binder twine manufacturers in Canada will be compensated for the disadvantages under which they labour.

The hon. gentleman, even as he reads that language, vindicates my statement. But if he will read the preceding remarks, he will see that I described the condition of affairs in the Philippine Islands, and stated that the compensation was to be made equal to the disadvantage.	*
The hon. gentleman did not say why or how.

The binder twine people were not concerned in the how or the why. I am dealing with the remark of the hon. member for Cardwell (Mr. Johnston) who said the binder twine people had no intimation. He is mistaken.
Would the Finance Minister tell us whether, in his opinion, this bounty will increase the cost of twine to the farmers ?

My hon. friend has worked that old gag often enough.
I do not pretend that the bounty increases the price of anything, and nobody else pretends it would. While a bounty would, of course, not increase the price to the consumer, the imposition of a customs duty might, and in most cases would, increase the price.

The hon. gentleman will permit me to say that I did not expect a gentleman occupying the position of Finance Minister would stoop to that low manner of addressing this committee, and using language of that kind. I do not wonder for one moment that the dignity of this House is going dowTn under such leadership. Would

the hon. gentleman be good enough to answer my question that he is so clever about ?
I did answer the hon. gentleman's question.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, he did not answer my question. What I want to ask the hon. gentleman is this : Will the hon. minister tell this committee, whether, when this bounty is placed on binder twine, it will increase the cost of binder twine to the farmer ?

No, I believe that in fact it will reduce the cost of binder twine to the farmer, but the question as to what is the effect of a bounty and the question as to what is the effect of a duty are vastly different things.
I did not ask that question.
I know the hon. gentleman did not ask it, but I took pains that he was not permitted to put a catch question without getting a fair answer.

I have no disposition to put a catch question. That is not my aim. 1 thought the hon. Minister of Finance, as he had introduced this motion, was the proper person to ask that question. I thought the committee had the right to the information that the hon. gentleman has tendered, and I am glad to see the hon. gentleman stand up and say that protection does not increase the price to the consumer.
The hon. gentleman has proved that he did intend to ask a catch question.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased, even at this late hour, to hear the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) state that it is not the intention to raise the price of binder twine to the farmers. The government have found out that the binder twine manufacturers cannot live without this bounty and they are going to give them a present of it. It will be stated throughout this country that this is designed to decrease the price of binder twine to the consumer, but the hon. Minister of Finance has proved to me that while this may be a benefit to the manufacturers, nobody else is going to get any benefit from it, because the government are not prepared to grant sufficient protection on binder twine to enable the manufacturers of binder twine to manufacture that article in Canada. While I am going to support this bounty, I do not believe that it is a proper way to put taxation upon the people. First you levy taxation upon the Canadian people to pay that bounty and then you leave an open door to the Americans to come in and slaughter their goods on the Canadian market. The argument has been presented that if we impose a duty upon American binder
twine the Americans may refuse to give us any manilla. Would the Americans give us any manilla now if they required it all themselves ? Everybody knows they would not. They have simply put that export duty on to help the Americans knowing that this government are pledged to meet their tariff on certain things.	[DOT]
Is it not a fact that the export duty on manilla affects the American people just as much as it does the Canadians ?
How does the export duty affect the American manufacturer ?
It affects the manilla going into the United States as well as to manilla coming into Canada.
There is no bounty in the United States.
There is a rebate.
As 1 understand the hon. Finance Minister they give a rebate on all that is manufactured in their own country.
On all that is exported.
Both lion, gentlemen are right. The duty is first imposed in the Philippine Islands and they get a rebate on all that is manufactured in the United States.

So that the American trade are assured of their raw material and this government has not backbone enough to stand up and put a tariff on binder twine sufficient to protect the Canadian manufacturers, but they give the Americans access to our markets to enable them to slaughter their goods and to crush the Canadian manufacturers. To illustrate my point let us suppose that I have ten head of 'cattle in a field and that my neighbour has twenty-five. Will I throw down the fence and allow my neighbour to pasture his twenty-five head of cattle in my field because I have only ten heads ? That is on the same principle exactly. We are levying a tax on the Canadian people to pay to the manufacturers of binder twine and then we are allowing the Americans to come in on the same ground and get the benefit of what they are doing. Why not impose a tax on the American producer for the benefit of the Canadian manufacturer ? I think I have used as much binder twine around sheaves as any hon. member of this House and I can tell the committee that when the tariff was taken off binder twine we paid more for it. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) has pointed out that the Americans have control now of our factories, so that the Americans can actually get this very bounty that we are giving to-day if they buy up the Canadian product. To-day I the market is full of American manilla on

which this bounty is given. The binder twine industry, if it so desired, might go on and manufacture binder twine in advance of the requirements of the trade and collect this bounty and they could sell out to the Americans and the Americans would get the advantage of the bounty.

Mr. Chairman, as I represent an agricultural county, perhaps it would not be amiss to say a few words on this subject. I am sure the farmers of my county will beg to be delivered from such friends as the hon. gentleman from Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte). He tells us that their interests will be best conserved by a protective tariff. I think he would have to hunt a long time in my constituency before he could find one farmer who would take any stock in that. The hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) made two rather surprising statements, as coming from an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House. One was that the government had cut down the tariff on a great number of articles. We have heard from these hon. gentlemen that the government had not affected the old national policy in the slightest. The statement of the hon. gentleman seems to me somewhat surprising. He made also another startling suggestion in the interest of the farmers, and that was that the Canadian manufacturers should be given control of the Canadian market. Let me illustrate what that means. I will take one class of manufacturers and I will Show how they deal with the country. I have under my hand some papers. I will take hardware for instance: cut nails, wire nails, tarred paper, pressed spikes, tacks, lanterns, rope, lead-pipe, shot, bolts and nuts, tire bolts, screws, carriage bolts, sleigh shoe bolts, machine bolts, blank bolts, bolt ends, varnishes, shovels, coach screws, wire of all sorts, nuts, axes, wooden-ware, haying tools, handles of all sorts, tinware, galvanized ware, wire doors, wire screens, coal hods, stove-pipes, elbows, locks and knobs, scales, papers, white lead, burst, putty. There is an association of these gentlemen, and I mean to say to this House that no wholesale dealer in Canada can buy a dollar's worth of these articles from any one of the members of this association until he enters into a binding agreement that he will not purchase from any other parties outside the association, that he will not sell for a less price than that dictated and then they will not really sell him the goods, but they will allow him a return commission for selling them. They dictate the price at which he shall sell them, and compel him to buy from them and after that they require him at stated periods, each year, or each six months, or each month, to make a statutory declaration that he has performed all these conditions. Let me read to the House from one of the letters I have, an extract from a contract that they require the dealer to Mr. JOHNSTON (Cardwell).
enter into. This is the statement of the shot men, and I will refer hon. gentlemen to the well known firm in Toronto of Jenkins & Hardy, who are the agents for a number of these concerns.
SHOT. *
January 8, 1903.
Dear Sirs,-We beg to advise you that subject ito the following conditions, you may be entitled to a premium of 2i per cent upon the net, amount of your purchases of shot (commencing to-day) in each six months ending June 30th, and December 31st, same to be payable within thirty days after the expiration of each six months upon which premium applies.
I am in the hardware business.
What manufactury are you connected with ?
I am a dealer in hardware, and in that statement you have read they stipulated nothing about the price that the shot shall be sold for.

I have yet that to read, and if my hon. friend is a retailer I may say that this does not apply to him at all. It refers to the wholesale man who stands between him and the manufacturer, and the wholesale man has to run the risk of his Insolvency. That is what 1 am getting at: Here are the conditions :
Conditions.-That we receive from you after the end of each six months period, ending June 30th, or December 31st, declaration which satisfies us that in the six months upon which you are applying for premium, you have not imported or purchased shot from any manufacturer other than those whose names appear below. and that you have not directly or indirectly offered or sold shot at less than the established prices of the Shot Association of Canada to the retail trade, or upon more favourable terms to your customer than the established terms of the said association to the retail trade.
We reserve the right to revoke and cancel all or any part of this proposition at any time on notice to you by registered letter of our desire and intention to do so, but not thereby to relieve ourselves from any obligations which may have accrued on your above described purchases of shot up to date of said revocation.
Those are the conditions which are imposed and if the hon. gentleman doubts m.v word he can go to the well-known firm of Jenkins & Hardy and he will find that such Is the case. I have the form of declaration which is required from these wholesale firms every six months or a year as the case may be, and if they do not make it they cannot purchase that class of goods from the parties who are in the association, and as far as I know and as far as I am informed and believe it is the case with every one of these manufacturers forms part of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I will state further that I have been informed and believe that the prices which are fixed by the Canadian manufacturers to-day throughout Canada for all hardware, are prices which are agreed upon by them in conjunction with the American

Manufacturers' Association. Not very long ago I chanced to hear a conversation which was taking place between a strong supporter of the Conservative party, a wholesale merchant, and another gentleman, aud he made this statement :	It is no use for us
to talk about it ; we in the wholesale trade are absolutely at the mercy of the manufacturers of Canada and they are in affiliation with the manufacturers of the United States.

If the Canadian manufacturers are in combiue with the American manufacturers and if the combination spreads over this continent, what difference would it make whether the duty was 25 per cent or 50 per cent, if the prices are regulated by the combine ?

I will tell my hon. friend that I believe that these manufacturers and these associations have ways and means of accomplishing their purpose that he does not know of and that I do not know of. I am prepared to accept the statement of the hardware merchant made in my hearing, and I know he is a man who knows what he is talking about, and he certainly is not a supporter of the present government.
Has the hon. gentleman drawn the attention of the Minister of Justice to that, and asked him to prosecute under section 520 of the Criminal Code V I did

If the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) is responsible for bringing that to the notice of the Minister of Justice, and thereby causing the section in the code referred to, then I say he has accomplished a great good to the country, because it should be a crime that these men may combine to absolutely control the wholesale business of this country, and to say to the wholesale merchants : You shall not buy merchandise any longer except from us ; we alone will supply you, and we will compel you to sell them at a certain price, and we will not permit you to sell at a lesser price, and we will dictate to you what the price shall be. The hon. gentleman has accomplished a great good if he suggested that to the minister.

I brought it to the attention of the Minister of Finance sometime ago with reference to the leather trade which is exactly on the same lines.
member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith) would say to us that we should deliver the whole of the markets of the Dominion of Canada into the hands of such men. I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, it is time for us to consider this matter. In my judgment the Canadian Manufacturers' Association have gone as far as they should, and they are trenching upon dangerous ground when they try to press on a bit further. I have only referred to the case of the hardware manufacturers, but I am informed that other manufacturers have been imposing the same conditions. Why, I went into an old established hardware concern not long ago and they told me that the Manufacturers' Association had actually sent a man to them demanding that they should have inspection of their books, because they had heard that the firm had purchased goods from concerns other than those in the association. I have a long string of names here, I do not w'ish to give them, but I thought it well to bring this matter to the attention of the committee.

In view of the long discussion of the subject aud the nature of that discussion, I would respectfully suggest to the Minister of Finance that he withdraw the resolution. It appears that this resolution which is intended to give certain relief to the binder twine manufacturing industry is not satisfactory to the friends of that industry who have taken a great deal of trouble to show that it is not sufficiently far-reaching and would not do any appreciable amount of good. That being the case, then speaking on behalf of those who use binder twine I can say that they are not asking for any such resolution, and I think the minister would please everybody by withdrawing the resolution and leaving the binder twine manufacturers just where they are now. I think, however, the discussion has done good in this way : that our friends opposite have taken a very definite stand upon the subject not only of the duties on binder twine, but on duties generally, and when the next election rolls around we in the North-west Territories will not be in the jjosition of being attacked because the government is too protective. We are at least saved from that hereafter because of the attitude taken by the opposition now and on previous occasions calling the government to account because they are not sufficiently protective. I am no sympathizer with the idea which has been put forward

All the credit to the hon. gentleman if he did that. It was time that some one should do it. And now we find that one of the leading gentlemen who has been asking us to care for and caudle the manufacturers in every possible way. has deemed it necessary in the interest of the public to cause an amendment to the Criminal Code of such a nature as declares their practices to be a crime. That is the position they are in, and yet the hon.
repeatedly by the opposition, that the remedy for all possible industrial and commercial evils is the raising of the tariff. It does not make any difference what the industry is ; it does not make any difference what tiie condition is. the remedy proposed in all cases by hon. members opposite is to raise the tariff. They speak for the people who are interested in raising the tariff and it is not at all wonderful that they should advocate that as a cure-all. I

speak for the people who are interested iu keeping the tariff low, and for my part let me say, that this idea that every inuns-try can be protected is a fallacy. If it is possible to protect every industry and if every industry is protected, it all comes around that no industry is protected and we are all on the same level. If there is to be protection some body must have the advantage and some body must be at a disadvantage or there is no protection. Protection means unfairness ; it means a special advantage to some, and unliss there is that special advantage there is no protection. In regard to this binder twine industry it has not received protection at the hands of this government. I take for granted that the government in framing the tariff came to the conclusion that somebody had to be sacrificed, that somebody had to get along with lower duties than other people had to. They figured no doubt that the great necessities of the country should come in under a low tariff or come in free, while the luxuries should pay the greater part of the revenue. On that principle, and considering that binder twine is a vital necessity to the greatest producing industry of the whole country; is an ever-recurring necessity and had been up to that time under the operation of a notorious combine ; the government placed binder twine on the free list. Taking into consideration the fact that the material entering into the manufacture of binder twine was entirely imported ; taking Into consideration the fact that there was a minimum amount of labour and capital entering into the manufacture of binder twine and a maximum amount of imported material, it seemed reasonable that that industry which had been the subject of the profitable operations of the combines for so many years, should be brought down to the level of no duty. There is no great capital invested in the manufacture of binder twine ; there is no large amount of labour engaged in its manufacture, at any rate, in proportion to the raw material used. The reduction in price of binder twine by reason of the abolition of the duty was a material advantage to the farmers of the country, and I am surprised that the opposition and some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House should take a stand in favour of the reimposition of a duty which, from the standpoint of the farmers at any rate, is an unjustifiable tax on his industry, a tax which is not supported by any of the reasons which can be advanced on behalf of some other industries. As my hon. friend from Wentworth said, the farmer is no pauper ; he is prepared to pay his share of the taxation of the country ; and give our hon. friends of the opposition any fair chance, and they will see to it that he pays, not only his fair share, but a great deal more. There are many articles of consumption required by the farmers on which the duty is higher than a revenue basis.

Probably the duty should be kept moderately high in the interest of industries in which there is a large investment of capital and a large employment of labour, In which native material and native labour enter largely or in which native capital, native labour and native material are the whole consideration. These industries certainly are entitled to all the benefit which a revenue tariff can give them. The farmers who are willing to submit to duties of this character, under these circumstances, are entitled to compensation of some sort ; and it was thought well by the government, in framing their tariff, to give them in the west compensation iu free binder twine, free barbed wire, free cream separators, and, in this eastern country, in free corn. The farmers have been given these advantages, which have been valuable, and I am glad, from a political standpoint, to see that our friends on the other side of the House have taken so long a time to-day, and have been so determined in their efforts, to establish themselves in the position of demanding that these advantages should be taken from the farmers.
As to the charge that the reduction of the duty has increased the price of binder twine, I do not suppose that anybody holds that seriously. Although It was proclaimed on every platform occupied by Conservative orators throughout the North-west at the general elections, we have had it on authority to-day that the reason of the increased price of binder twine was the war in the Philippines, which enabled the binder twine factories to pay a dividend in one year of 100 per cent, in another year of 40 per cent, and I am told in two other years 20 per cent ; and the lowest they have paid since 1896 has been 10 per cent. I would like to know what these binder twine companies want. They have made more profits, from one reason or another, in spite of, if not because of, the removal of the duty than possibly any other manufacturing industry in this country. Surely this is an industry which, in the first place, it is an advantage to the farmer should not be protected ; and, in the next place, it surely is an industry which could and should live without protection.
There are certain disadvantages under which the binder twine companies in Canada labour, as compared with their competitors in the United States, in connection with this export duty on manilla. For one, I am prepared to say that if the bounty proposed to be given to these industries is not satisfactory to them, if it is not enough to relieve them from the control of the United States combine, of which complaint has been made here to-day ; if it is not enough to put them on their feet and enable them to pay 100 per cent dividend every year, then I think the government would be justified in withdrawing the resolution and leaving them exactly where they stood before. Rut if the

question is raised as to the principle or the theoretical right of imposing this duty, I think that question is very easily answered. There are certain conditions existing beyond the authority of this country which produce a certain set of conditions in this country ; and it is no contravention of free trade, or of any other reasonable doctrine of government, that action may fairly and properly be taken in this country by any means possible to meet those conditions.
Another apology.

No apology whatever ; a complete justification. It is the business of this government, or of any government, to see that the various industries of the country are not placed at an undue disadvantage because of the action of other countries. In this case they have seen fit to take special means to do it. But, for my part, I say that if they did not see fit to do so, and if, because of that, the binder twine industry went to pieces altogether, it would still be better for this country at large that we should be able to import our binder twine free of duty than that this country should be taxed, on one hand to pay the rebate, or, on the other hand, to provide a duty that would enable the price of binder twine to be raised to the consumer in this country for the profit either of the United States combine or the Canadian combine.
Has the hon. gentleman the courage to move a resolution carrying out the views he has just expressed ?
It is hardly necessary for the hon. gentleman to ask that.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his authority for speaking of a Canadian combine ?

I am given to understand that the great reason for the demand for the reduction of the duty in 1891 was that it was understood that a Canadian combine existed. My own experience does not go back to that time ; but that I am given to understand, and I believe it is true.
Does the hon. member believe there is one yet ?

From what the hon. member for St. Slary's said to-day, that the American combine came into this country and dictated terms to our manufacturers, under which terms our manufacturers restricted their output, and I believe paid their shareholders dividends ranging from 10 per cent to 100 per cent, we are entitled to say that the binder twine industry is a combine which is a part of the American combine : and I do not see how that condition would be improved to the consumer by the imposition of a duty, which would simply enable the members of the Canadian combine to take that much more out of the Canadian consumer.
We have heard a great deal with reference to the manufacturers and the industrial classes of this country. Surely the real industrial class, which produces the great wealth of this country, is entitled to some consideration at the hands of this House. The hon. member for St. Mary's drew attention to the exodus of Canadians to the United States and demanded that there should be an imposition of duties to prevent that exodus. Another hon. member drew attention to the necessity of imposing duties to prevent the recurrence of hard times in Canada. When did Canadians go to the United States most rapidly, and when were times hardest in Canada ? When the duties were highest, and under that government whose policy was called national, which was to put the duties just as high as the manufacturers asked.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The statistics do not prove that. They prove the contrary.
Well, I am sorry for the statistics, that is all. Does the hon. member deny that the exodus of Canadians to the United States from 1878 to 1896 was greater than ever it was before or since ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr.. OLIVER. He denies that. Then the United States statistics do not bear him out. Does he deny that times were harder in Canada during the regime of the Conservative ministry than they were before or since ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes.

Everybody denies it.
Mr. OLIVER, Then my hon. friends are very good deniers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: From 1874 to 1878 we had the worst times we ever had.

The hon. member (Mr. Oliver) would not get credit for sanity to talk in the country in that way.
Mi-. OLIVER. I have heard a great deal about those hard times from 1874 to 1878. It is not within my memory that they were anything like what hon. gentlemen opposite asserted.
Is it not within the knowledge of the hon. member that during the Mackenzie regime the government appointed a commission to inquire into the causes of the prevalent depression at that time ?

Possibly they did. But what I wanted to ask these hon. members was this : Do they admit that times were hard in 1S96, or were times prosperous then? Silence gives consent. Times were hard in 1S96. The so-called national policy was in force and the Conservative government was in office. It was within their power, if they had the will, to place duties on any

article at any rate they pleased. If they did not exercise that power and improve the times, it could only be because they did not believe what they say now, or else that what they say now is not true. There is no getting away from that proposition.
Mr* CLANCY. The only way to get away is that these are fairy tales.

There is no fairy tale about the fact that trade in Canada has more than doubled since the lower tariff came in force ; there is no fairy tale about the fact that the population of Canada has greatly increased since that time ; there is no fairy tale about the fact that while Canada was manufacturing millionaires from 1878 to 1896 and the bulk of the people were poor, to-day the bulk of the people are growing wealthier, and for the last seven years we have not heard so much about millionaires being turned out.
They have gone broke on stocks lately.

There is no use in lion, members telling this House or the country that a mere increase of duties is going to increase prosperity. Our memories are short, but they are not so short as that. If an increase of duties generally will, produce general prosperity, I am for increase of duties. But the experience of eighteen years proves that high duties cannot produce prosperity. It is only a waste of words to tell us that a repetition of these duties will make the country generally prosperous.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question ? How is it that the city of Toronto, which certainly has more manufacturing concerns than all the rest of the province of Ontario, has increased within the last ten years upwards of 100,000 in population, while the whole province has increased only 50,000, and nearly two-thirds of the counties of Ontario have decreased in population in the last ten years 5
I really do not know. If the people are not there, they must be some place else.
They are going to the United States.
They have gone to Manitoba and the North-west.

In regard to the movement of population, I want to say to hon. mem-' bers in all earnestness that during the years of the so-called national policy, during the years of unreasonably high duties, which laid burdens upon the farmers for which they received no compensation, there was a movement of our population from eastern Canada to the North-western states to such an extent that to-day the state of North Dakota is practically Canadian, the state of Minnesota the Red River valley is large-

ly Canadian, the state of South Dakota is largely Canadian, and the states of Washington and Oregon have large numbers of Canadians among their population. You say : These people went from a country of low protection to a country of high protection. That is true. But had it not been for the protection that prevailed in Canada, including the North-west, which placed our North-west at a disadvantage, all things considered, as compared with these Northwestern states, our people would have gone to the North-west and Canada would not have lost that population.
They went from a high protection country to a country of higher protection. How does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) explain that consistently with his theory ?

It was because of the greater proximity of the western states and easier means of reaching them, coupled with maladministration in the Canadian North-west which made the North-western states seem desirable by comparison.
That is not an answer to my question.
Well, I am doing the best 1 can for the hon. gentleman.
Speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite such as the hon. gentleman is now making drive them over to the United States.

No danger of that. Let me tell the hon.. members that the truth underlying this demand for increased duty on binder twine is practically this-that the farmers are prosperous and can stand it. That is really the argument underlying this demand. But the farmers could not stand it from 187S to 1896, and they cannot stand to have a similar condition of affairs introduced again. The question is not whether they are willing to stand it or not. The fact is they cannot stand it. When you put ia great industry-the industry upon which the whole prosperity of the country depends-at a disadvantage, you necessarily injure the minor industries, including that of manufacturing.

I do not mean to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I would like to ask a question in all earnestness. Does he say that in the thriving west peopled with probably the most enterprising farmers in Canada, ruin would follow the imposition of a duty of 12} per cent on binder twine ?
Did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) understand me to say so ?
Quite so.
I fear the hon. gentleman's hearing cannot be good. I certainly did not say so.
What is the hon. gentleman's argument then ?

My argument is that if hon. gentlemen opposite were allowed to bring in their policy of laying the burden upon the farmers for every line of industry and consumption, they could not stand it. They could not stand it before, and they cannot stand it now.

The reason I asked the question is this-the only relief the hon. gentleman can point to as having been afforded the farmers of the North-west with respect to duties is the abolition of this twelve and one-half per cent on binder twine. If the prosperity of the North-west is due to a change of tariff, and the only change affecting the North-west is this twelve and one-half per cent on binder twine, then, according to the hon. gentleman this change has brought about that result.
The hon. members opposite are the authority on the subject of tariff changes. I am not presuming
Let the hon. gentleman answer that.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) say that the abolition of the duty, twelve and one-half per cent on binder twine is the only change in the tariff V
The only substantial change affecting the North-west.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman, and, as we do not agree upon our facts, we can hardly reach an agreement in our conclusions. If there has been no substantial change in the tariff except this twelve and one-half per cent on binder twine, what are the hon. gentlemen talking about ? If we have the same tariff as they had. why should they complain V Will they come forward as one hon. member did on their side and say-while another repudiated his statement-that we must have tariff for tariff with the United States ? Will they say that we must have not a protective tariff, but a prohibitive tariff ?
What is your position ?

I believe in a low tariff. If hon. members insist that there has been no substantial reduction in the tariff, they can mean nothing by their proposals of change except to have prohibition instead of protection. I shall be glad if they take that stand and stick to it. We would like to go before the country with them on that question.

I wish to make representation to the minister with respect to the material entering into the manufacture of binder twine-if we may return to the que-s-^on of binder twine for a moment. As 1
understand it, the bounty is to be paid on binder twine a large factor in the manufacture of which is manilla. I am informed by a constituent of mine, who has invested his money in this industry, that he is able to produce a fibre from another material that will be a substitute for manilia. I would ask that, if this can be made a success, the bounty be applied to binder twine made of this new fibre. The hon. gentlemen have appointed Mr. Joseph Haycock as inspector of binder twine. I am sure that Mr. Haycock, who has a great knowledge of the trade and of the requirements of the farmers, would be able to say whether the article produced by this fibre was as good as that into the composition of which the manilla has entered. May I ask the minister's consideration of that point, and that the bounty may be made applicable to the product I refer to.

I can promise consideration of that for the future, but we could not bring it into operation immediately.
Mr. TAYLOR, I want to ask the minister, in view of the statement made by several hon. gentlemen opposite that they believed this bounty would reduce the price of twine to the farmers, why it is that he has made this measure retroactive, and gives a bounty on binder twine produced since the first of September last ? He must know that the manufacture for the present year is now over, and every pound of twine that is being manufactured in Canada has been sold to the retail men, who have probably sold the greater portion of it to the farmer. How is the farmer going to get any benefit, unless he amends his resolution so that the manufacturer who is to get the bounty reduces the price of that he has already sold to the retailer, and the retailer remits the amount of the bounty to the farmer ?

The farmer gets the benefit in the reduced price that the American is able to sell his twine for. and our people have to come down to that. It is to enable our people to come down to the American price that this bounty is given.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That is in prospective, but the last year's output is sold on the market and there is not a merchant in Canada today who has a stock in store. Half the crop in the western country has been harvested with the binder twine, and how are the farmers going to get this rebate ? It is simply a bonus taken out of the labouring men and given to the binder twine manufacturers ?

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 233) respecting the manufacture of binder twine in Canada.
