speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first and second time, and House went into committee thereon.
' Mr. CLANCY. I would like to ask the lion, gentleman how he proposes to deal with the twine that has been sold and passed out of the hands of the manufacturers V

In every matter of this kind there are some possible difficulties. We shall have to deal with it by the general power of making regulations applied to all other bounties. I have no doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has charge of that branch of business, will be able to devise means. That is the only answer I can give my hon. friend.

The hon. gentleman ;vill admit that in asking the assent of the House to the Bill he ought to be able to give his reasons now. This is a very difficult question to deal with. The whole outi>ut of twine since September, 1902, nearly a year ago, has passed entirely out of the hands of the manufacturers.

It is to be paid to the manufacturers of binder twine. I think I am correct in stating that although sales of binder twine have been made of late, probably there had been few if any sales made prior to the date of the announcement made in this House. There is no doubt that the transactions that have taken place during the current season have been based upon the expectation that this bounty will be paid. The manufacturers understood they would receive it, and whatever effect that has upon prices lias gone into operation.
Mr. CLANCY'. Does the hon. gentleman say that he has given the manufacturers an intimation ?
No, I did not say that. I gave the manufacturers no intimation except that which was conveyed to the public on the floor of this House.

The contracts for twine were made chiefly long before the budget was brought down. I think the most difficult proposition is to find, out how much was manufactured, because it has passed out of the hands of the manufacturers. How are you going to arrive at the amount of money you require to give as a rebate ?

I do uot think it is important whether it has passed out of their hands or uot, for the purposes of this Act. They are entitled to a bounty by way of compensation for the duty which they have paid, and every pound of twine manufactured for the present season, as we are advised, that which has been manufactured from manilla, has paid the export duty, and that is the basis upon which we

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: propose to make the compensation. As to ascertaining the exact amount, that is a matter which will probably have to be based upon the returns made by the manufacturers, returns that they will make in good faith and upon affidavits. The importation to deal with the quantity of manilla which has been imported for all purposes, and some factories use manilla not merely for binder twine but also for cordage. It may be difficult to distinguish. I confess I do not see anything we can do but to accept the affidavit of a reputable manufacturer. We have to do that in customs duties every day, and I suppose we shall have to do it in this case.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The manufacturer fixed his price last March, and most of his orders were taken from the retail merchants for the quantity they required in March. The sale was based on the cost of the product, the export duty that he had to pay, the labour and everything else. He sold it then, not expecting any rebate from the government. He has got his money for it, and now the government are making him a present. I do not see how the farmer is going to get any benefit from it.

This may help the manufacturer of twine, but it will not help 1 he man who bought the twine. I am told that a great deal of the twine manufactured in Canada this year has been bought up by American firms and is distributed through their own channels. Take, for instance, the McCormick Manufacturing Company. They bought up large quantities of Canadian twine so as to control the market, and they distributed it to their own customers. Certainly it could not be expected that we would have any very great sympathy with the American who bought that twine, but he sold out to the retail dealers, and the retail dealers, upon the basis of that price, sold to the farmer. The farmers will get no advantage this year from this bounty, whether they do next year or not. There will be some twine manufactured yet, because they keep manufacturing until towards the end of the harvest. Small orders are coming in at the present time. When I was home a week ago some men had not enough twine to keep them running more than two or three wreeks, and they could not get any until the manufacturer had provided more twine. Others got twine from the McCormick Company, who have collected it in Canada and distributed it both from Chicago and from points in Canada. This is going to help the manufacturer, but for the present it will not help the farmer. I want to say one word in regard to what the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) said that if this is undesirable why not withdraw it. We do not say that it is undesirable; at least I do not. I say it is good as far as it goes, but in my judgment it does not go far enough, because we want a duty im-

posed as well. As far as it puts our manufacturers in tire same position as the American manufacturers as to raw material, I think it is right, but I think the government ought to invoke the criminal code to break up what is in reality some kind of an understanding between the manufacturers of binder twine in this country and the American handlers of that article, and to break up some of the combines in the handling of iron and steel.

The explanation of the proposal is this :	The
American manufacturer, when he was manufacturing binder twine without the added cost of the export duty, might manufacture it cheaper than if he had to pay the export duty. The export duty was put on, he had to pay it, but he got a rebate. Having obtained that rebate his twine would cost so much less under that condition of things. He then would fix his price taking all these matters into consideration. Having fixed his price and coming into competition with our manufacturers, our manufacturers, of course, would have to regulate their price in Canada with his price ; so that, they would be at about f of a cent per pound disadvantage and the farmer would get the benefit of that.
How V

The American manufacturer could sell his binder twine cheaper because he had got this rebate. The Canadian manufacturer, not having obtained that rebate, would nevertheless have to sell his twine at a price to meet the the price of the American manufacturer, and this bounty is to compensate the Canadian manufacturer for the loss he would be at as against his comjoetitor In the United States. The farmer got the benefit of the lower price that had been fixed in the United States by virtue of the rebate that the American manufacturer had got. That is where the farmer gets his benefit. The farmer was buying his twine under absolutely free conditions and one of these conditions was that the men in the United States who sold it to him had 1 of a cent per pound rebate, so that they would be able without any sacrifice to give the advantage to the farmer because the Canadian price had to be fixed in competition with the price of the American manufacturer, and it is to compensate the Canadian manufacturer that the resolution has been introduced.

Although the American manufacturer gets his manilla free, and although he is manufacturing under these conditions he is fixing the price of binder twine in our country to-day. How is the Canadian farmer going to get any reduction in price on account of this bounty, when the price is fixed by the American manufacturers '!
If the American manufacturer did not get a rebate-
We are giving it to the Canadian manufacturer.
The hon. gentleman asked me a question and I am answering it. If the American manufacturer did not get a rebate of the export duty his binder twine would cost him g of a cent per pound more.
Who are you giving this rebate to V
To the manufacturer of binder twine in the United States.
You are giving it to the manufacturer in the United States ?

We are not giving it ; the American government are giving it to the man who manufactures binder twine in the United States. He has paid the duty and he gets a rebate. If he did not get that rebate his binder twine would cost him 9 of a cent per pound mare, but as he gets that rebate he can sell his binder twine at 9 of a cent per pound less. The Canadian farmer in importing this binder twine is able to import it from the United States at 9 of a cent per pound cheaper that he otherwise would he able to do. The Canadian manufacturer who has to sell in competition with the American manufacturer must sell, having regard to the import price, and must pay 9 of a cent per pound in addition to his cost and we are giving him back that 9 of a cent per pound by way of a bounty.

I had expected a better course of reasoning from the lion. Minister of Customs than that. I am not going into an intricate debate of the question, but. I am going to ask the hon. gentleman if the American gets a rebate on 15,000,000 pounds of twine that comes into Canada, how is the Canadian consumer interested in any sense in this bounty that we are giving ? He will get his twine at the reduced price that the American sells it at, by reason of his getting the rebate. I am prepared, even to take a wrong course to help the manufacturers out of the deal that was put upon him by hon. gentlemen opposite, but I deny that the consumer benefits to the extent of one farthing.
Not by this.
This is not intended for him, this is for the manufacturer.

I admit the manufacturer will benefit by it because he is obliged to pay the fine in consequence of the action of hon. gentlemen opposite that the Americans have imposed upon him. The hon. gentlemen give the Americans free entry into our market. But the Americans were not satisfied with that. They fine any man in Canada who wanted to manufacture

binder twine in his own country, 3 of one cent on each pound that he brings in, and that is the result of the action of lion, gentlemen opposite. They are now' imposing a tax upon every man, woman and child in Canada to the extent of the. bounty on binder twine to help our manufacturers out. but the consumer in no sense gets one farthing in benefit. Yet that was the argument that the hon. gentleman made just a moment ago.
An lion. MEMBER. No, no.

The lion. Minister of Customs says that the farmer will get his binder twine that much cheaper. The farmer gets it that much cheaper because he is not depending upon the Canadian manufacturer for a pound of his twine. He will get every pound of it under conditions tnat lion, gentlemen opposite opened up to him by means of giving the Americans complete control of our own market and if the American manufacturer gets a rebate in his own country because he sends his twine to this country, then, our farmers are in no sense concerned in this bounty. They are only concerned inasmuch as they must put their hands in their pockets and pay for it. As a usual thing, a duty has to be paid by the consumer. There are cases where the consumer pays the duty, and there are cases where he dees not. There are cases where the party pays it, and where he partly pays it, and where the exporter from a foreign country partly pays it but in this case it is unerring. It comes out of the pocke'ts of tlie people, whether they use binder twine or not. The hon. gentleman will ask me what my position is. 1 take the position that on general principles bounties are wrong. There are some eases where they would be justified. They are only justified where the conditions are such that reasonably, protective and defensive duties are inadequate to give our own people a fair field in their own country, but whenever you withdraw duties, or a defensive tariff, from a certain industry in Canada and give a substitution by compelling our own people, consumers or not, to pay tribute in that way, I think you adopt the most mistaken policy that could be pursued in any country. The hon. gentleman knows that this is a compensation for his own blunder. He knows perfectly well that if the government had retained or advanced the duty he would not be coming down now and ask big the people to put their hands in their pockets to pay bounties. I am not going to object. He has made the most of it, and I am willing as a tax-payer in a small way to contribute my share to help the manufacturers out until such times as we have a government that will relieve them of this burden that has been placed upon them.

The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that we are not depending, under the conditions created entirely by himself, upon the Canadian manufacturer for one pound of twine. I repeat that I am astounded beyond measure that the Minister of Customs should present the argument that the farmer gets no benefit from that. The farmer is not obliged to buy one pound from the Canadian manufacturer. Whether they put two cents a pound upon the raw material that comes into Canada, and whether or not we can get it elsewhere, the farmer has not a particle of concern so long as the Americans can come into this country and sell all the twine.
Suppose we took the hon. gentleman's plan of putting three-eighths of a cent on binder twine, who would pay that ? That is the point.

I will give my hon. friend a candid answer. The American manufacturer would not want that three-eighths of a cent put on, because it would place him at a disadvantage. The American is opposed to it for some reason, and the reason is that it would probably cost him that three-eighths of a cent to get in to this market. I will say that there might be a slight advance, but I do not admit it
Take one position or the other. Would the farmer pay anything of that or would he not V

The foreign producer of hinder twine is opposed to our raising the duty, and if we pay the duty he need have no concern. Will the Minister of Customs say that if we put a duty of three-eighths of a cent a pound the Canadian farmer would pay it all ?
I have asked you a question, and what is your answer ?

I have told the hon. gentleman that the chances are to a large measure that that three-eighths of a cent would be paid by the foreign producer who wished to get in to our market. Now let me ask if the Minister of Customs will say that the American producer would pay none of that duty, and that the Canadian consumer would pay it all.

We all know very well as to the question of who pays the duty ; that circumstances govern. Let me ask the hon. gentleman this : Canada is short 13,000,000 pounds of binder twine, and that has to be got somewhere, and that being the case, let me ask the hon. gentleman if under these conditions the Canadian farmer would not of necessity largely, if not wholly, pay the duty ?

That is a very fair question. If we are 15,000,000 pounds short by reason of the policy of the government which has closed up our binder twine factories, I am prepared to admit frankly that the farmer would pay it because the government has cut off the source of supply in *Canada.
We have more manufacturers of binder twine now than we had at the time the hon. gentleman is speaking of. '

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where is the output ?

Coming from the factory.
Mi-. CLANCY. The hon. gentleman well knows that the inci'ease in our production of binder twine has not kept pace with the increasing demands of the country. 1 admit that under the conditions which the government has created our farmers might have to pay the duty, but if we produce our own binder twine there would be no such condition as the Minister of Customs pictures.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Minister of Customs has said that there are more binder twine factories in Canada now than bef re the duty was taken off. Let me tell him that the output of the Canadian factories to-day is less than half what it was a few years ago.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Y'es it is. Your factory and one or two others are making a little, but where are the factories at Toronto, at Cobourg, at Pert Hope and at Montreal and at the Kingston penitentiary ?

Busy.
Mi'. TAYLOR. Y'es, but they are making rope and not binder twine. When the Minister of Customs announced that binder twine would be on the free list he said that the American manufacturers could come into our country and sell their twine, and that the Canadian manufacturers could go to the United States and sell Canadian twine. But the Minister of Finance admitted to-night that we imported over $1,000,000 worth of twine from the United States and our Canadian manufacturers had not been able to sell a pound over there. When the minister brought down his tariff resolution, why did he not provide that American twine could come into Canada only when our twine could go into the United States 1 That might have been a sensible thing to do. A few years ago they called these manufacturers bloated monopolists, but to-night they are giving them a bonus which will go to the manufacturers and which will not go to the consumers. They endeavour to compensate the manufacturer for the loss he has sustained, because the American government give a bonus on what is exported out of the country equal to the duty they pay on the man-ilia coming from the Philippine Islands. There is the position the Minister of Customs has got the manufacturers of Canada into. When he brought down the tariff he said to the Yankees :	you can make tw'ine
over there and sell it in Canada and we will have the right to make twine in Canada and sell it to the United States, but when we went to sell our twine there they would not let us in. Every farmer in this country knows that ever since this government came in the price of binder twine has been increasing. At first they blamed it on the war, but last year they had not that excuse, and from the accounts of the Kingston penitentiary, which show what they paid for their raw' material last year, we know that the farmers of Canada paid 12 and 13 cents a pound for their binder twdne, when it only cost one cent a pound to manufacture it. We know' that the Canadian industry is in the hands of the United States combine and that they dictate to our manufacturers the price they' shall charge and the quantity they shall turn out, or else the Americans will lower the price and crush every Canadian factory, there being no duty to protect them. We know that every Canadian dealer had to place his order and did place his order w'ith the McCormicks, and other American firms, who sent an agent over here, and they . placed their orders in March last for the

quantity of twine they would require. Therefore nobody will get the benefit of this bounty except those bloated manufacturers that the Minister of Customs a few years ago used to be blowing about. Now he is giving them a bonus out of the treas-uary of this country as he admits. Why should he ask the workingmen of this country to pay a bonus on binder twine that is used only by the farmers. The farmers do not want the poor workingmen to contribute to the price of their binder twine, and it is unfair for this government or any other government to tax the workingmen to lower the price of binder twine for the farmer, and that is what it amounts to.

It is a pity that in discussing a matter of this kind we do not get to the exact facts. My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) conveys the impression that our binder twine factories are entirely closed up, and apparently doing nothing. We are not in a position to say exactly how much binder twine is made by the Canadian factories, but one way of getting at it is to ascertain the amount of raw material that is imported into this country out of which this twine is made. In 1898 we imported $572,000 worth ; in 1899, $941,000 worth ; in 1900, $944,000 worth ; in 1901, $076,000 worth ; and last year $1,290,000 worth, being the largest importation of the raw material out of which binder twine is made that we ever imported into this country.
Will the hon. gentleman give us the quantity in pounds ?
I cannot tell you that.
The price has increased nearly double.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And this covers all the cordage besides ; it is not binder twine alone.

So it does, but we have the right to assume that if in 1S98 we imported $572,000 worth of raw material, and last year $1,296,000 worth, there must necessarily have been more binder twine made last year than there was in 1898.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is double the price it was then.
No, it is not.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Pretty near it.

There were a few statements made here to-night that ought to be referred to in the interest of the binder twine makers of this country. It has been represented that they are dictated to by the foreign manufacturers. The statement has been made by the hon. member for St. Mary's that they are only permitted to make a certain quantity and if they attempt to make more they are threatened with being wiped out. I have some knowledge of the binder twine business in this country ; I know the Mr. TAYLOR.
men who carry it on, and I do not believe that statement is true. I believe that the hon. member for St. Mary's has been so informed by parties who are desirous of having the duties restored; but I do not think the statement is correct, because I know that the binder twine companies to-day are trying to turn out all the binder twine they possibly can make. The great complaint of the manufacturers of binder twine is that the United States manufacturers, protected by a duty of 45 per cent upon all twine of which manilla is a component part, have absolutely the American market to themselves, and at their own convenience fix the prices at which binder twine is to be sold. Our people early in the season are not aware of the quantity that is likely to be imported into Canada, and they are afraid to manufacture largely because they do not know what the requirements of the United States will be. If there is a large harvest such as there was last year, a*d a large demand for binder twine in the United States, the surplus which the United States manufacturers will have to dispose of will be considerably diminished, with the result that the price will be kept up. But if, unfortunately, with the producing capacity of the American binder twine factories equal to or more than equal to the consumption, there should be a small crop in the United States, and a large output of binder twine, the American producer, who is not prevented from coming into Canada, will be forced to sell his binder twine here at reduction ou the American price probably of two cents, which would immediately take away all the profit and part of the principal of the Canadian manufacturer. Therefore, the Canadian manufacturer wants a duty to protect him from that competition. It is undoubtedly the fact that the American manufacturer has his own market to himself. It is unquestionably the fact that lie fixes the price for the Canadian consumer by dictating the price at which the twine shall be sold in this country. The American manufacturer supplies first Texas and then the other wheat regions of his own country, gradually coming north ; and if at the end of the season he finds that he has mors twine than he can sell in the United States, he can under present conditions invade the Canadian market, and by selling his twine at two cents a pound less' than ho does in the United States, he can undersell our producers, and thus, by making money on the American side and losing a little on our side, he ruins our industry.
Would the hon. member be kind enough to tell us what amount of American twine was imported into Canada in 1896 and in the present year ?

Last year there was imported $1,500,000. The American importations into Canada are growing larger every year.

lion. Mr. HAGGAIiT. In 1896 there were 4,000,000 pounds, if I recollect rightly, and this year 15,000,000 pounds.

The importations are undoubtedly increasing, and the position is this, that the United States manufacturers, beiug able to manufacture their binder twine at the very lowest cost, owing to the fact that they have the largest establishments for the production of the twine, are placed at a slight advantage over our people, which is compensated for by the fact that our people can hire their labour at a little less cost, and can distribute their twine through the agency of farmers' associations who are associated with them. That puts the two pretty nearly on a par ; and if our people had a protection of 12i per cent, they could prevent that slaughtering which may take place at any time whenever there is a surplus of twine in the United States. The fear of that surplus constantly presses on our manufacturers of binder twine. The result is that at those seasons of the year when they ought to be employed in producing for the Canadian consumer, they are afraid to produce, not knowing the amount of surplus that there will be in the United States. Therefore, they limit their production, and thus increase the manufacturing cost of the product. Of course, hon. gentlemen are aware that I am in favour of a duty on binder twine. Having two binder twine factories in the city of Brantford, I am naturally a little more interested than people from other localities.
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of it because he has a couple of factories in his constituency or because he believes it to be right ?

Of course, I think that binder twine should not be singled out from the operation of a revenue tariff ; but having these factories there, I am a little more conversant with the conditions that exist in reference to binder twine, and I wish to say that all the statements that haave been made here with reference to a combine in Canada are incorrect. No such thing exists. The majority of these binder twine factories are owned by farmers. There are over thirty thousand farmer stockholders.
I did not say there was a combine. I said the price was regulated from the American side.
That is so.

I applied to two dealers, one of them bought from McCormick, and the other from Deering, and I asked them if they could not get the twine cheaper from our own factories. They said they were informed by these factories that it was utterly impossible, because the American manufacturers struck the prices.

cost the country a great deal more money than the bounty will cost the farmers. At any rate, it shows the disposition of the government, that our manufacturers shall not be subjected to unfair competition, and I look forward with confidence to the time when a revision of the tariff shall take place under the auspices of the present Minister of Finance, and when, I believe, ultimate justice will be done to the manufacturers of binder twine in this country.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I made a statement awhile ago which some lion, members appeared to doubt. I have here the Trade and Navigation Returns for 1895. I find that in that year we imported from the United States 2,035,785 pounds of binder twine. Last year we imported about 15,000,000, or eight times the quantity imported in 1895. The value of our imports last year was given by the Finance Minister at a figure which shows a valuation of over 10 cents per pound. In 1895 the value of our imports was $123,315, or a fraction over 6 cents per pound. I said the price last year was nearly double that of 1895, and here is the proof of it. In 1895 Canadians were making their own binder twine, and selling it at about 6 cents per pound ; but this year we are getting our binder twine, or at least three-quarters of it, from the United States, and, as I stated, at nearly double the price.
When was the export duty placed by the United States on raw material for binder twine ?
I think in March of last year.

A great deal of the twine manufactured since September of 1902 is made of raw material that was imported before the imposition of this duty. How is the hon. minister going to arrange in his Bill or regulations to provide for that ? Will it apply only to raw material imported since the duty ?
Yes.
But the resolution does not provide for that.

I think the hon. gentleman will find that that is fully covered. It says :
Such bounty to be equal to the amount paid as export duty in the Philippine Islands on manilla fibre produced in such islands and used in the manufacture of binder twine in Canada.
Certainly, our intention is to do what the hon. gentleman suggests, and our regulations will be made so as to carry it out.
The hon. gentleman says that the Bill is the same as the resolutions, and he will see that the resolutions do not cover the point.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is mistaken.
But certainly that Is the intention, and I think he can rely on the regulations being made accordingly.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why is it that the Canadian manufacturer is under some disability in not being able to sell his product in the United States as the American sells his product to Canada ? I understood that an arrangement was made under which binder twine was to pass across the boundary either way.
I am not aware of any such arrangement.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That was the impression that was left.

In view of the statement of the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) that a combination exists and prices are fixed by the American interests, I would like to know if the Dominion government, who manufacture binder twine to a certain extent, were a party to that combination ?

I am afraid the hon. gentleman will have to bring that forward when the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) is in his place. He is in charge of the penitentiaries where the twine is manufactured, and he is the com-binester if there is one.

When the hon. gentleman used the phrase ' prices are fixed,' what I meant was that they are fixed simply because the Plymouth Company and the Harvester Company sell in the United States and Canada at certain prices, and our people are compelled to sell at the same prices, or they cannot sell at all. There is no combination.

It would appear that the Canadian government has been a party to some combine or conspiracy to charge the farmers more for their binder twine than they ought to pay. The hon. member for South Brant has stated that the Farmers' Binder Twine Company made enormous profits, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 240 per cent, besides using large amounts of their earnings to add to their plant. So they must have made a profit of over 300 per cent. Yet farmers are not able to buy from the Dominion government for less than they could buy from Canadian or American companies. I find that according to the Auditor General's Report for 1902, volume 1, page M-47, that farmers were charged 104 cents for mixed manilla, which was sold by the government for five and one-tenth to the jobbers. In answer to a question asked him this session of parliament, the hon. Minister of Justice said that this twine was made for about six cents per pound. If this twine can be made for six cents per pound, why does the government charge

the Canadian farmer ten and a half cents per pound ? A margin of four and a half cents is more than a reasonable margin, and would go to show that there was a combination to which the Canadian government was a party.

I suspect that the government sold binder twine at the trade price. Had the prices gone down they would have had to face the loss, and as it went up, they did not find reason for departing from the trade price.

It would appear that there is a combination and that the government are a party to it. They do not sell to the farmer at a fair advance on the cost of production, but they sell at the same price as the others.
I hope so.

This is an injustice to the farmer. The factory at Kingston was not established for this purpose. When the manufacture of binder twine in Kingston penitentiary was determined on, it was in order that twine might be sold to the farmers at reasonable prices. Yet, if the hon. minister's statement is correct, the object now is to sell at the same prices as are charged by other manufacturers. To charge the farmer 41 cents profit on binder twine made in the penitentiary, an unreasonable profit, and one that goes to show that the government are a party to the combination.
I would suggest that the words 'imported since March, 1902' be inserted after the words 'paid as export duty in the Philippine Islands on manilla fibre produced in such islands.'

I do not like to make changes in this way. But I will give consideration to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman and will consult the Minister of Justice about it. If the section is not clear as it stands, I will make it clear either with the form of words the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) suggests or with some other.
Bill reported.
